#4427. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

That is a funny picture with the tiny 500e "pulling" that huge trailer.

But on a more serious note, there's so much that goes into pulling. It's control. It's stopping. It's being smart enough to watch the weather forecast and know when to pull off the road and sit out a storm.

The irony here? Back in 2004, I began working at a dealership selling Chrysler, Dodge, Ram and Jeep. So of course we had the big trucks and many came in buying the 2500/3500 with the Cummins Diesel. Chrysler Corp made every sales person go through specialized training for the trucks and towing. Every sale had to include a form signed by the customer about towing and the limits of the truck they were buying. Hidden in there was a clause that stated the customer would NOT use the truck to tow more than the listed (legal) amount. If the customer didn't sign it, we were told by Chrysler that would be a no sale. They were very serious, and for good reason.

I may not like seeing all these huge trucks on the road. But when it comes to towing, mass is your friend. A powerful engine, huge (good) brakes and a well trained driver are a must.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4426. Honda Just Teased a New Hybrid SUV Called the Avancier

The revived nameplate is expected to debut in Thailand next month as Honda prepares a major expansion of its hybrid lineup.

Honda is reviving the Avancier name for what looks like a new SUV, as first reported by Automotive News, suggesting the model could play a role in the automaker’s renewed push into hybrids.

Honda posted teaser images of an all-new Avancier on some of its global social-media channels, showing a sharply styled vehicle with slim taillights connected by a full-width light bar. The company has not released any specifications, but the teaser confirms that the Avancier will be one of the first models to use Honda’s new-generation hybrid technology.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 17403

The Avancier name has been used twice before. Honda originally sold it in Japan as a wagon from 1999 to 2003, then revived the name in 2016 for a larger, more upscale Chinese-spec crossover. The new version appears to be headed in a different direction than either, with reports pointing to a three-row SUV slotting above the CR-V, though none of those details have been confirmed by Honda.

Thai media reports say the new Avancier will make its world debut at the Thailand International Motor Expo on December 1.

More important than the nameplate may be what’s under the hood. Honda announced last month that it would call its next-generation hybrid system “Honda Hybrid,” with global launches beginning in 2027. The automaker says it plans to introduce 15 next-generation hybrid models worldwide by the end of fiscal 2029, with North America a primary focus.

Honda says the new hybrid system is designed to cost more than 30 percent less than the system introduced in the 2023 Accord while improving fuel economy by more than 10 percent. The system uses a redesigned engine and hybrid drive unit and can be paired with a newly developed electric all-wheel-drive system.

That strategy represents a big shift for Honda. Like many other automakers, Honda had been pushing aggressively toward EVs, but changing market conditions have prompted it to put more development resources into hybrids. Honda plans to make all of its North American auto plants capable of building hybrid vehicles and expects to launch larger hybrid models in the region beginning in 2029.

Whether the Avancier will come to the United States remains unclear. Honda has not announced U.S. availability, and the company has previously indicated that some next-generation hybrids will be tailored to specific markets. For now, the Avancier appears to be an early look at the new direction of Honda’s global hybrid.

#4425. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

PHEV. With 200miles of range. More than decent, but for the most part what I would have loved in 2015. Less so now.

Still, for the price that is very decent electric range. And it looks good too.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

#4424. BMW’s iX5 Beat The Lucid Gravity On Highway Range. Not On Efficiency

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW’s answer to electric SUV range anxiety involves a battery big enough to make some other EVs look underfed. The new iX5 packs 144 kilowatt-hours of usable capacity, which gives it an EPA range of 435 miles. But EVs can’t typically match their official range claim when driven at a constant 70 mph on the highway.

The iX5 came very close to matching it in this Out Of Spec Testing group range test, though. It covered 410.8 miles, putting it ahead of the Lucid Gravity Grand Touring, Rivian R1S Dual Max, and Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric. It wasn’t the most frugal SUV here; it simply combined respectable efficiency with an enormous energy reserve.

There’s an asterisk next to that headline range number, though. The BMW initially shut down at around 400 miles (644 km). However, they were able to get it moving again, which unlocked enough remaining energy to keep going at highway speed and extend the range.

Video host Kyle Conner notes that the BMW initially shut down after going through almost exactly 144 kWh, its stated usable battery capacity. At that point, it had been showing 0% remaining in the battery for around 10 miles.

Restarting it added another 4 kWh, allowing it to continue at 70 mph (113 km/h). Kyle speculated that the car might deliberately stop after delivering its rated capacity, leaving some remaining energy accessible after a restart, but stressed that this was a theory rather than a confirmed explanation from BMW.

The Lucid Gravity Grand Touring finished second, covering 367.7 miles (592 km) at 70 mph (113 km/h) with its 123-kWh battery. The Rivian R1S Dual Max followed at 349 miles (562 km), although the testers extracted only around 136 kWh from its aging pack (it had nearly 30,000 miles on its odometer), versus roughly 145 kWh in an earlier test. The Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric finished last at 309 miles (497 km).

We’ve seen the Gravity miss its EPA figure on the highway before. In a previous test, it recorded 345 miles, although Lucid flagged a possible rear drive-unit problem with that vehicle, which may have affected the result. Different conditions and test endpoints also mean those results aren’t directly comparable.

Porsche, meanwhile, puts more emphasis on how its SUV drives than outright efficiency. The Cayenne Turbo Electric brought a performance-focused powertrain, 21-inch aero wheels, and a towing package, yet it still used less energy per mile than the BMW. Its limiting factor was the smallest battery here at 108 kWh, despite showing higher efficiency than both the BMW and Rivian; it finished roughly 102 miles behind the winner.

The iX5’s win here is convincing, even considering the restart. The Gravity squeezed more miles out of each kilowatt-hour, but the BMW simply had more of them to spend. Sometimes the answer to range anxiety really seems to be just a bigger battery.

#4423. Riot Reveals Full League of Legends Conversion, But You’ll Have to Wait

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

All the time, live service titles are forced to pump out content to avoid stagnating over time, anything to catch the attention of new players and reignite the passion of old returning faces. Sometimes, games feel the need to really shake things up, especially if they’re on the older side of release dates. Today, it seems, League of Legends is joining this number.

Stats for Star Wars Zero Company are out, and the results are showing some major Clone supremacy.

Announced at the tail end of Worlds 2026, Riot has showcased what it calls “League of Legends: New Dawn”, a total revamp of League’s client, mechanics, and visuals to bring it up to snuff with the modern age.

All these changes and more have been requested by the community for years, but now that they’re right around the corner, a vocal segment seems incredibly unimpressed.

League of Legends is a title that has slowly but surely been pulled down by the weight of its ancient code, forcing the dev team at Riot to totally rewrite decent chunks of the client inside and out to make new proper content. This hiccup has been the excuse for missing features and slow updates for ages, and it looks like Riot is finally ready to put their foot down.

With a new proper rival in the MOBA space via Valve’s Deadlock, Riot has had a bit of a fire lit under them, pushing them to speed up development in this massive overhaul. New runes, new lobby animations, and a fully reworked map are just some of the new content coming in this proper total overhaul of the game, looking to lead League into a New Dawn for the coming years.

It seems like every member of the classic League roster is also getting a full visual overhaul, bringing them up to the quality showcased by recent releases like Locke and Zaahen. Compounded with the rumors of a sequel series to Arcane in the works, it seems like Riot is focusing hard on celebrating and bringing focus back to base League of Legends, rather than highlighting the universe with different titles.

Sometimes, games feel the need to really shake things up, especially if they’re on the older side of release dates

Riot stayed vague on a lot of the actual reworked mechanics, but with 2 minutes of footage out and a promise of more coming in January, current players and fans who have fallen off the wagon both have a reason to keep an eye out. They say League comes for every PC gamer eventually, and a few good changes could make its tendrils all the harder to avoid.

A sizable amount of the community response to the announcement has actually been rather negative, tossing shade towards the game for looking too “mobile game-y” after its vibrant new coat of paint. This marks a phenomenon I’ve seen throughout longtime free-to-play titles: a confusing mix of wanting developer attention without actually wanting much changed.

The Counter-Strike community is another proponent of this practice, clearly wanting Valve’s attention through skins and patches, without actually wanting any real part of the CS tempo changed. Now, for longtime fans, this can be understandable; after all, nobody wants their favorite game suddenly changed into something totally different. However, every live service title, no matter the age, needs new blood.

The aging visuals and code of League have clearly been the largest stopgap to its constant evolution, and the promises set forth by Riot for League of Legends: New Dawn are seriously hopeful, opening the door for new players and those who have grown tired of the shakiest part of the MOBA giant. Years of work and slow improvement are clear through every inch of the visuals, I just need to see how it plays!

#4422. We Explored the Ford Vault, the New Home of Ford’s Heritage Fleet

From classics like the Model T to concept cars and race cars, the Vault is full of wonders.

Up until recently, Ford didn’t have an official collection of its many important historical vehicles. That all changed when Ford started curating its Heritage Fleet in 2024, and we got our first sneak peek at the collection in 2025. Now, however, Ford has moved the fleet into a new permanent home: the Ford Vault.

Situated in a nondescript building in Romulus, Michigan, the Ford Vault will house the Heritage Fleet, which includes everything from Model Ts and Mustang prototypes to race cars and one-off concepts. Currently, due to zoning laws, the building is only open to employees and offers limited opportunities for media, with the site formerly used as an Amazon warehouse.

However, Ford promises that it is working with the Romulus city government to get the building up to code so it can be turned into a public museum. The company didn’t provide a timeline for when the collection would open up to the public, but we got to take an early look at the fleet it has amassed.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 20147

Many of the cars were already part of the collection that we saw back in 2025, but Ford also brought in several new vehicles. We’re not going to cover any of the vehicles we wrote about back in 2025, so if you’re interested in what else Ford has in its Heritage Fleet, go check out that roundup below.

See More Cars from the Ford Heritage Fleet

Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts, but this one stands out for two reasons. For starters, this Model T was sold in the United Kingdom, meaning it has the steering wheel on the right. You’ll also notice that instead of the customary black paint job, this Model T wears a vibrant green hue. Henry Ford’s famous line of “any color, so long as it’s black” didn’t actually come into effect until 1914, once the groundbreaking assembly line was up and running. Before then, you could order the Model T in red, green, blue, and grey. Black paint dried faster, leading Ford to restrict the color palette once the assembly line was bustling for the sake of efficiency.

The Super Chief concept is the complete opposite of the bare-bones Model T. Designed as a vision for a luxury truck in an era when pickups were transitioning from workhorses to lifestyle vehicles, the concept took inspiration from the Super Chief locomotives of the 1950s for its domineering look. Under the hood, it used an innovative supercharged 6.8-liter V-10 called “Tri-Flex” because it could combust gasoline, E85, or hydrogen. Coach doors open to reveal a decadent cabin covered in brown leather, brushed aluminum, and American walnut wood. The glass roof sits over a structured grid of leather and wood, while the bed is lined with wood and strips of metal.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 20147

From the front, this may look like a normal Mustang GT350, but once you get to the rear, you’ll find that it has actually been converted into a pickup truck. This Mustang Ute project was built by apprentices in Ford’s metal shop at its Experimental Vehicles Building as a way to train them on the complexities of building concept cars. It uses the bed from a Ranger, and while it was never destined to be more than a training exercise, the Ute now has us daydreaming about a hi-po successor to the Falcon Ute sold in Australia until 2016.

The Model T isn’t the only foreign-market car in the collection. This is the adorable first-generation Ka, a tiny hatchback sold in Europe from 1996 to 2008. In fact, this was the final first-gen Ka to roll off the production line, and it has fewer than 10 miles on the odometer, making it probably the most pristine Ka in existence. The Ka was a big success for Ford, and it even spawned a convertible called the StreetKa, which we’d love to see added to the collection in the future.

Ford has called its upcoming Fathom electric truck a “Model T moment,” but this isn’t the first time the company has employed such language. The 2003 Model U concept was designed as a modern take on the Model T’s “people’s car” approach. It was a small pickup truck that could be transformed into an SUV via a retractable rear section. It also had a retractable canvas roof and exterior body panels made from a soy-based material. Under the hood lived a supercharged 2.3-liter four-cylinder hydrogen-combustion engine mated to an electrified automatic transmission. The Model U got a claimed 45 mpg and was loaded with features that weren’t yet common in 2003, from a head-up display to adaptive headlights and automatic emergency braking.

The Ford Bronco was killed off in 1996, but by 1999 there were already plans to bring the off-roader back. Designer Moray Callum led a team that proposed this next-generation Bronco, known under the codename U260. It was based on a Ranger platform, but never progressed much beyond this exterior-styling prototype. Ford would revisit the Bronco in 2004 with a concept that debuted at the Detroit auto show, which also lives in the Heritage Fleet, but we’d have to wait until 2021 to see the Bronco name return on a production car.

Love it or hate it, the SYNus is certainly one of the most unique-looking vehicles to ever wear the Blue Oval. While it looks like it should be pronounced like “sinus,” the name is actually meant to be said “sin-you-ehs,” combining “synthesis” and US, standing for “Urban Sanctuary.” The design looks like a bank vault on wheels, with thin windows, slab-sided bodywork, and even a wheel handle for the rear door. While it looks imposing in photos, the SYNus is actually quite small in person, only measuring 158 inches long. It was powered by a 134-hp 2.0-liter four-cylinder mated to a five-speed manual.

These days, Lincoln only sells SUVs, but back in the ’90s, the luxury division considered building a two-door roadster. The L2K began as a proposal for a Mercury sports car, before Ford brass changed their mind. Built on a heavily modified chassis from a 1993 Mazda Miata, the L2K packed a 250-hp 3.4-liter V-8 engine and a four-speed automatic. The L2K was a drivable concept, and it reportedly completed around 100 laps of Saugus Speedway in Santa Clarita, California. It then debuted at the Los Angeles auto show and toured the show circuit before management scrapped the project. While there were reports that the L2K was scrapped, the slinky Lincoln clearly survived.

This pointy concept from 1963 is actually based on a Shelby Cobra, eschewing the iconic curvaceous body for a wedge shape. Designed by Eugene Bordinat, Ford’s head of styling at the time, the Cougar II’s fastback fiberglass body looks sleek and modern, with a rich red paint job accented by chrome trim. The Cougar II also wore pop-up headlights, and improved aerodynamics meant it could allegedly hit 170 mph (10 more than a standard 260 V-8-powered Cobra). The Cougar II and a similar concept, the Bordinat Cobra, are on loan from the Detroit Historical Society, and the Ford Vault may include more vehicles on loan for rotating exhibits once it opens to the public.

Many of Ford’s concept cars feature experimental powertrains, and the Reflex is no exception. This futuristic-looking compact coupe was motivated by a diesel-electric hybrid engine with innovative-for-the-time lithium-ion batteries. Ford claims the Reflex could return 65 mpg, and with an electric motor on the rear axle providing all-wheel drive, 60 mph arrived in a claimed 7.0 seconds. Opening the rear-hinged butterfly doors reveals a cabin that looks inspired by athletic wear, with lightweight seats upholstered in mesh and rubber in the floor taken from Nike shoes. The Reflex also has a 2+1 layout, with a single “love seat” mounted behind the front passengers, along with an integrated child seat and a baby camera monitor mounted in the dash. Sadly, this mixture of sporty and practical never made it into production.

We’ll close with a trio of vehicles that won’t be in the Vault beyond the next few days, but are too good to not include. These are the three Ford GT40 race cars that, somewhat controversially, crossed the finish line together to take the top three spots at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans. The legendary finish saw the black No. 2 Shelby American car driven by Bruce McLaren take first place ahead of Ken Miles in the blue-and-red No. 2, who had been leading for much of the race’s final hours and had been asked to slow so that the three leading GT40s could finish together.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

#4421. BMW Just Started Making EV Batteries In America. The New iX5 Will Be First In Line

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW’s first high-voltage battery factory for electric vehicles in the United States is now up and running in Woodruff, South Carolina. The facility, which is located just 15 miles from the automaker’s car factory in Spartanburg, will supply finished battery packs for no fewer than six Neue Klasse EVs assembled in the U.S., starting with the new iX5 SUV.

According to BMW, the new facility doesn’t build cells from scratch. Instead, it sources ready-made cells from local suppliers, which are then checked at the plant under a “zero-defect” policy. BMW says it will source Gen6 cylindrical cells from LG Energy Solution in the U.S., while Samsung SDI will supply European factories.

BMW EV battery factory in Woodruff, South Carolina

After analyzing each incoming cell for voltage and other parameters, the factory starts the clustering process, where the battery cells are connected to coolers to ensure optimal insulation and cooling. While the packs go down the assembly line, they are continuously monitored in real time to make sure that each pack goes out the door in tip-top condition.

The company’s latest EV batteries are built using the “cell-to-pack” technique, where cells are no longer arranged in modules. Instead, they’re put directly into the pack enclosure, where they’re protected by a hardened foam. This way, more cells can fit into the same volume, leading to more energy density and more driving range.

In South Carolina, all production staff go through a virtual reality training program, so they can practice real manufacturing operations under realistic conditions before they set foot on the assembly line. What’s more, BMW is relying heavily on artificial intelligence-powered digital assistants and more than 250 robots to output zero-defect batteries. Over 300 employees are currently working at the company’s new battery-making facility.

The Woodruff plant is BMW’s fourth site in its Gen6 battery production network to start series production, after the facilities in Debrecen, Hungary, Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Germany, Shenyang, China, and San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

It took the automaker roughly three years to go from groundbreaking to mass production in South Carolina. Construction of the Woodruff plant began in September 2023, and just one year later, in September 2024, the first manufacturing equipment was installed. In summer 2025, the first pre-series batteries rolled off the assembly line.

What makes the new facility special, besides being BMW’s first battery plant in the U.S., is that during normal operation, it doesn’t use any fossil fuels, with the site’s industrial trucks being powered by hydrogen. As for the latest Gen6 cylindrical cells, they’re touted as having 28% fewer carbon dioxide emissions compared to the cells used in the outgoing iX SUV.

#4420. Comparison Test: 2026 Jeep Recon Moab vs. 2027 Rivian R2 Performance

Two squared-off electric SUVs square off.

Normally, it’s easy to identify an incumbent. Establishment figures tend to enjoy advantages—experience, name recognition, resources—that are scarce for upstarts. But in the case of the 2027 Rivian R2 and the 2026 Jeep Recon Moab, it’s hard to say who’s the incumbent and who’s the challenger. Jeep has been building SUVs since the 1940s, as it’s happy to constantly remind you, but is relatively new to EVs. Meanwhile, the first Rivians hit the road just five years ago, but EVs are all that it builds, and the R2 is the brand’s third model. Which incumbency is more advantageous? Let’s take a look.

The fresh-out-of-the-oven R2 hews to the typical launch strategy of offering the most expensive version first. Thus, our 2027 model is a Performance trim with the Launch package, which brings a 4400-pound tow rating and hands-free driving assist. Simpler variants are coming soon, priced closer to 50 grand, but our tester with its $2000 Launch Green paint tallied $61,485. Happily, the R2’s most delightful feature, its power roll-down hatch glass, is standard. Sorry, Toyota 4Runner, Rivian is onto the lifestyle appeal of a dropped rear window with a surfboard poking out. Or a dog or two who won’t be breathing exhaust fumes.

See all results for new 2026 Jeep Recon EV for sale near 94043

The Recon is so far only available in Moab trim, which at Jeep signifies elevated off-road capability along with an elevated price. Indeed, the Recon’s $68,990 base sticker exceeds the R2’s as-tested figure, and an assortment of goodies further inflated our as-tested price to $73,345. Major options included the $1995 Comfort package, which adds ventilated front seats and heated second-row seats, and the $995 towing package (max capacity: 3300 pounds). Plenty of off-road hardware is standard: skid plates, an electronically locking rear differential, and 33-inch all-terrain tires. And because Jeep is leaning into the “Wrangler, but electric” theme, the Recon’s doors and rear windows are removable without tools. But, at about 70 pounds each, the doors might not be removable without a daily swig of creatine.

The R2’s styling is “Honey, I Shrunk the R1.” It’s clean, modern, and employs the signature Rivian ovoid headlights. There’s nothing too revolutionary about it, but that works to its advantage—Rivian wants to sell the hell out of this thing, and divisive styling is not a smart play for conquesting market share from internal-combustion rivals. (Just ask the Tesla Cybertruck.) And, hey, you can’t go wrong with big wheels pushed out to the corners. Our tester had all-season tires on 21-inch wheels, the mall-crawler spec, but Rivian does offer tougher-looking 20-inch wheels with all-terrain tires. Those, however, will drop EPA-rated range from 330 miles to 307 miles.

See all results for new 2026 Jeep Recon EV for sale near 94043

The Recon’s aesthetic is intentionally anti-EV, with nary a concession to aerodynamics or rolling resistance. It’s square, tall, and has a front bumper that looks like a bulldog’s underbite, all of which contributes to an atmosphere-battling 0.404 coefficient of drag. It doesn’t quite pull off the Wrangler’s studied minimalism, but the Recon is the most off-road-forward EV this side of a Hummer or a Mercedes-Benz G580e. It’s also capable of changing up its look, depending on whether the doors and windows are removed. Buttoned up, it’s a regular SUV with an off-road bent, but ditch the doors and open the full-length canvas roof, and it’s like you’re driving something from the car-stripping contest in I’m Gonna Git You Sucka.

Inside, the R2 and Recon represent their respective manufacturers’ design philosophies. Whether you prefer the spare, screen-centric Rivian or the more conventional Jeep is a matter of your priorities (and, maybe, age), but the Recon is undeniably more user-friendly. Stellantis may whipsaw on its product planning—EVs! No, V-8s!—but its interiors are consistently good, from Jeep to Ram to the Chrysler Pacifica. A splash of tan leather across the top of the steering wheel matches the seats, and a red panel on the console draws attention to the rocker switch for the terrain modes. Both the Rivian and Jeep feature large touchscreens, but the Recon augments its touchscreen functions with hard buttons (on both the dash and the steering wheel) and knobs for volume and tuning. The Jeep’s Uconnect 5 system also supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, while the Rivian doesn’t allow phone mirroring.

Rivian minimizes physical controls in part by aping Tesla’s strategy of forcing scroll wheels into multiple roles. Want to adjust the steering wheel or exterior mirrors? You’ll need to go into a settings menu in the touchscreen and temporarily deputize the steering wheel scroll wheels (“haptic halo wheels,” in Rivian parlance) to handle whichever adjustment you’re pursuing. It’s annoying, but probably not the kind of thing you deal with too often as an owner. At least, while you’re wrestling with that, you can gaze upon the lovely birch trim that spans the dash.

Both interiors allow a view of the sky, with the Rivian employing a fixed panoramic glass roof and the Jeep offering the full convertible experience with its power roll-back soft top. The R2 can also drop its windows (including the back one) with the touch of a button—the rear quarter windows stay fixed, alas. You can remove those in the Recon and, unlike the doors, store them in the car in handy bags. In any case, both SUVs are down with al fresco travel, but the Recon is more committed. The catch is, you’ve got to be committed too.

The Recon and R2 both showcase the hyperbolic performance we’ve quickly come to regard as the EV norm. Why, some of us are old enough to remember when the C5 Corvette Z06’s sub-four-second run to 60 mph was considered wickedly quick. And now we have family off-roaders that will torch that Vette—and plenty of other sports cars besides. To wit: The R2’s dual motors combine for 656 horsepower and 609 pound-feet of torque, good for a 3.5-second 60-mph time and an 11.4-second quarter-mile at 126 mph.

HIGHS: Removable doors and glass, quicker than a Charger Scat Pack, real off-road ability.LOWS: 160 miles of real-world highway range, higher price, Wrangler people will probably leave ducks on it.VERDICT: Jeep’s EV off-roader is fun and fast but far from frugal.

The Jeep is even more powerful, and its huge Nexen Roadian ATX tires are churned by 670 horsepower and 620 pound-feet of torque. The Recon ties the R2 to 60 mph and is slightly behind in the quarter-mile, requiring 11.8 seconds. The Jeep’s quarter-mile time is compromised by its 111-mph speed limiter, which it hits more than a second before it finishes the quarter. And still, it runs 11s. If you’re wondering how quick the Jeep would be minus the doors and glass, superleggera-style, so did we. And we’ll let you know the answer to that next time we get our hands on one.

The Jeep’s 94-kWh battery is bigger than the Rivian’s 88-kWh pack, but the Rivian’s superior efficiency means that it goes longer between charges. In our 75-mph highway range test, the R2 managed 260 miles, a full 100 miles more than the Recon. It also charged a little bit faster, going from 10 to 90 percent charge in 39 minutes, versus 43 minutes for the Jeep. If you’re not doing 75 mph, the Recon fares somewhat better—its EPA-estimated range is 222 miles—but it’s still well short of the 300-mile threshold that’s become a common range expectation for EVs.

Neither the Rivian nor Jeep are particularly impressive dynamically, but as with range, you can divine their handling prowess just by looking at them. On the skidpad, the Jeep holds on for 0.74 g of grip, while the Rivian ekes out 0.81 g. The R2 also out-stops the Recon from 70 mph, 178 feet to 201 feet. We’d guess both those differences would be narrowed if the Rivian wore its available all-terrain tires, but both machines are like old-school muscle cars—hellaciously quick in a straight line but not about to hang with a Mazda Miata in the corners.

Although our two contenders here are calibrated more for on-road comfort than apex-slaying performance, the Recon is far more competent and composed than the Wrangler that it’s cosplaying as—an independent front suspension and rack-and-pinion steering work wonders to modernize the Jeep driving experience. It’s tall, yes, but you don’t get the sense that you’re heaving around in the crow’s nest of an 18th-century schooner, nor does it impart the side-to-side neck snap that presents when overly aggressive anti-roll bars begin asserting themselves. The cushy ride is helped by the all-terrain tires’ generous 70-profile aspect ratio. You won’t likely bend a Recon rim on a pothole or a rock out on the trail.

HIGHS: Stupidly quick, looks great inside and out, the rear glass rolls down!LOWS: Lack of physical controls, light regen setting still too strong, no CarPlay or Android Auto.VERDICT: A premium SUV for the masses that happens to be electric.

Many of us feel the R2 is better to drive than its big sibling, the R1S, despite having a simpler suspension setup with conventional anti-roll bars. The R2 feels like it had plenty of R&D attention, in accordance with its importance to Rivian’s business model. Specifically, the spring and damping rates feel in harmony, with firm body control but enough compliance to soak up nasty pavement. There’s no sense of the suspension abruptly running out of travel, either on droop or compression.

Both the Recon and R2 feature some mandatory brake regeneration when you back off the accelerator, but the Recon’s is milder and feels more like coasting compared to the Rivian’s system. Rivian really wants you to embrace one-pedal driving—in fact, it insists. We’re still not sure why Rivian is so big on mandatory regen, but if you like your car to coast down hills (which, as we’ve explained before, is more efficient than converting kinetic energy to electricity and back again), then the R2 might be a little too one-pedal for you even in its weakest mode.

We didn’t get to really off-road the R2 and Recon, but that contest might be closer than you’d think. The Jeep takes its off-road mission seriously, with 9.1 inches of ground clearance and those 33-inch tires, but the modest Rivian actually has more ground clearance (9.6 inches), and its 32-inch tires aren’t much smaller. Speculatively, they’d both be fun to take muddin’.

The Recon is quick and charismatic, but its high price and stunted range make us think that Jeep built this model as an EV beachhead rather than as a serious volume contender. It’s also better at being a Jeep than it is at being an EV. If you wanted an electric Wrangler, this is the closest thing to it, for now. You can drive it in Mad Max dune-buggy mode, and strangers will leave ducks on the windshield, but the Recon is a fun idea that’s desperately awaiting the next generation of batteries to extend its range. Put it this way: When you’re shelling out more than $70K, it hurts to get smoked on range by the $29,000 Chevy Bolt (262 miles, per the EPA).

So the R2 wins this contest because it delivers the design—and most of the performance—of the R1S at a much lower price point. It’s easy to build a compelling vehicle when you’re charging more than $120,000 (see: the R1S Quad), but it’s much more impressive when you’re targeting the high $60,000 range, the heart of the market. With more than 300 miles of EPA-rated range to go with its scalding acceleration, the R2 is the electric family SUV we’d want to put in our own driveway.

#4419. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

If you’re following the electrification of transport, the cheapest place to start is your own roof: home solar can power your EV for close to nothing. #4418. 10 JRPGs Launching in 2027 You Should Keep on Your Radar

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

The pandemic sure threw a wrench into many developers' plans, which was understandable. However, as soon as the situation began to normalize, many games that were delayed or suffered internal setbacks started getting revealed with official release dates. It feels like ever since 2023 we have been living through a run of great releases, with banger after banger.

Furthermore, JRPG fans have been well served since then. A new title keeps coming out, whether from indie developers, veterans who left their former companies to start their own studios, or fresh remasters and remakes popping up. I, for one, would love some peace and downtime to just play casually, and I thought 2027 would bring that relief, but I was mistaken. The year hasn't even begun, and my backlog is already clogging up again. Let us take a look at a few upcoming JRPGs in 2027 that you should definitely keep on your radar.

Which 2026 JRPGs are the best according to their Metascore?

Terranigma brings back a classic from the SNES, a JRPG that formed part of the legendary Quintet Trilogy. It functions more as a direct port than a full remaster, but it remains extremely welcome nonetheless. Terranigma never originally launched in North America, only in Japan and Europe, meaning many players from back in the day never had the chance to experience this action RPG.

In Terranigma, we play as Ark on a mission to restore Earth. And by Earth, I mean our actual planet, as all the continents are based on real-world geography that we gradually bring back to life. To do this, Ark uses a real-time combat system driven by level-ups and spells you buy along the way. The most enjoyable aspect of Terranigma is witnessing the world-building sidequests unfold as you visit villages and restore them. It is a fantastic treat for anyone looking to revisit or experience a past JRPG gem through an official release.

Against all odds and to my utmost surprise, SaGa is becoming one of the longest-running and most sprawling series in the Square Enix catalog. I know it is unorthodox and not everyone enjoys its unconventional design, but I love seeing Square keeping the franchise alive, especially through its remakes. Following Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven, Square Enix is delivering a full remake of the third entry titled Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United.

The remake will include similar enhancements to Revenge of the Seven, such as a revamped turn-based system that heavily emphasizes targeting enemy elemental weaknesses, while retaining core SaGa staples like Glimmer mechanics and open-ended progression where players shape the narrative path. I don't know if it will be as brutally difficult as the original Romancing SaGa 3, which was notorious for softlocking players with its complex progression systems. Still, it will certainly be a feast for fans of the series.

Continuing with upcoming remakes, Atlus is bringing another project to the table: Persona 4 Revival. As the name implies, this is a ground-up remake of the fourth Persona entry, fully modernized with current-gen graphics, overhauled combat mechanics, a re-orchestrated soundtrack, new social activities, extra story events, and expanded dungeon crawling elements inside the TV World.

The best part is being able to revisit what many consider the best Persona game (a statement that could honestly apply to almost any entry in the franchise). Returning to the town of Inaba, we play as the canonically named student Yu Narukami. While keeping up with his daily routine of school life, part-time jobs, and social simulation, he will also need to unravel the mysteries of the TV World alongside fan-favorite Teddie.

Atelier is one of the longest-running JRPG series, with a fanbase more dedicated than a football club. While the overall narrative remains anthological across the franchise, Atelier is organized into distinct subseries. Following the Secret subseries featuring Atelier Ryza, we have the Memories subseries, which kicked off with Atelier Yumia and now continues with Atelier Karia: The Night Kingdom & the Guide of Memories.

Atelier Karia continues the adventure in Aladiss, this time venturing into the underground world of Noctrem. This entry puts players in control of Karia, an amnesiac alchemist. Combat builds upon the real-time foundation established in Yumia, with Karia introducing a strategic layer that lets players pause combat to execute command skills or parry incoming enemy attacks. I won't say playing Atelier Yumia beforehand is strictly mandatory, but if you want full context, it might be the ideal route.

It's no exaggeration to say that Eternal Anima is one of my most anticipated JRPGs of 2027. The game was unveiled during a Nintendo Direct, and while I initially fell in love with its charming pixel art, it first looked like just another solid indie release. That changed once I looked into the talent behind the project, including industry veterans like Kazushige Nojima, a legendary Final Fantasy writer, and director Katsuhisa Higuchi, who worked as a battle programmer on several Final Fantasy titles and directed Monster Hunter Stories 2.

Early previews for Eternal Anima are singing high praise, spotlighting its refreshing turn-based combat, its time-travel mechanics (a narrative trope I never get tired of), and how seamlessly both elements interlock. The story follows Wade alongside an eclectic party gathered from different timelines. Combat features a mechanic called Future Sight that previews enemy moves, showing who they plan to target and the exact damage output, which elevates tactical planning and should be a joy to experiment with. I will be sitting in the front row waiting for Eternal Anima.

If you loved Final Fantasy Resonance, then it's time for more JRPG love, Jobs, and pixel art.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation needs no introduction and stands as one of the world's most anticipated JRPGs of 2027. We can wait for The Game Awards to hand out the Most Anticipated Game trophy, and if Final Fantasy VII Revelation doesn't take it home, feel free to call me out in the comments. Serving as the conclusion to the Final Fantasy VII remake trilogy, it appears to have refined everything that made its predecessors spectacular, pushing combat, exploration, and player freedom to new heights.

Narratively, it will conclude the main arc, though whether it introduces major plot twists remains to be seen. We do know the Weapons are present and look more imposing than ever. Combat introduces two new playable party members, Vincent and Cid, along with the new FITs system, which acts like a Job framework to give each character a broader tactical arsenal. As for traversal, with the Highwind at our disposal, Square Enix stated that world exploration is completely open, leaving route decisions entirely up to the player. Certain regions will have higher level thresholds, nudging players to tackle them later, but the overall scope looks immensely promising. Final Fantasy VII Revelation, the year is yours.

We now shift to games targeted for 2027 that lack specific day-and-date release slots, which leaves them open to potential schedule shifts. That said, if one developer rarely delays its titles, it is Nintendo. Because of that track record, when Nintendo announced Xenoblade Genesis for 2027, I knew with confidence I would be playing it next year.

Xenoblade Genesis marks the latest chapter in the Xenoblade saga. Whether it functions as a direct narrative sequel to the Chronicles arc remains unconfirmed, but it continues under the direction of Monolith Soft and series creator Tetsuya Takahashi. The reveal trailer omitted gameplay, focusing instead on narrative cutscenes that showcased story beats and main characters. The artistic direction initially drew mixed reactions from some fans for leaning closer to Fire Emblem than traditional Xenoblade, but I personally loved every bit of it, including the medieval aesthetic.

Knowing Monolith Soft, Xenoblade Genesis will feature a colossal world, an overhauled battle system, unorthodox progression mechanics, and endless features that will sink hundreds of hours into this new universe. Did I mention Yoko Shimomura is composing the soundtrack? That alone means it's a fantastic time to update my Spotify playlists.

In this new JRPG, players take control of Asch and Finé as they set out to prevent a world-ending catastrophe known as the Lightfall. Rev. NOiR. is an action RPG, but it features a tactical time-stop mechanic similar to Final Fantasy VII Remake, letting you pause combat to issue skill commands through a visually stylish menu. Deep gameplay details remain sparse for now, but as mentioned, I'm choosing to trust the project and will be ready on day one once Rev.Noir. locks in its official release date.

Here is another franchise that requires zero introduction. Pokémon Winds & Waves is being touted as the first truly high-fidelity graphical Pokémon title, which would certainly be a milestone achievement for Game Freak. Given its oceanic setting packed with islands and open seas, it has every tool required to expand the open-world framework of Pokémon Scarlet and Violet to unprecedented heights, complete with fresh traversal mechanics.

No specifics have been revealed regarding the battle mechanics. However, it will likely preserve the turn-based structure of its mainline predecessor while leaving real-time action gameplay to the Legends spinoff series. For anyone jumping into Pokémon Winds & Waves, three traditional elemental starter companions await: the puppy Pombon, the gecko Gecqua, and the bean chick Browt. I will almost certainly end up picking Gecqua.

I want to start by noting that, according to the developers and director Tetsuya Nomura himself, Kingdom Hearts IV will definitely launch in 2027 and won't face delays. Square Enix confirmed that internal development is progressing smoothly, setting up the long-awaited return of Sora's adventure in Quadratum, complete with new characters (along with returning faces for those who played the mobile entries) and a fresh selection of Disney worlds.

In terms of core design and gameplay structure, we can expect a polished take on the series' classic loop: Sora travels from world to world, adapts to local rules, meets regional protagonists, and aids them in their struggles. It is a charming formula, and I would not have it any other way. Officially, only the world of Coco has been formally revealed, though a leak stemming from Steam achievements unveiled several others. I won't share those details here to keep you safe from spoilers, but if you want to look them up, do so at your own risk.

From Eternal Sonata to Triangle Strategy, revisit seven underrated JRPGs that launched near major blockbusters and struggled for attention.

#4417. Tesla Model 3 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn't

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Everybody knows that electric cars are pretty easy on the owner’s wallet when it comes to regular maintenance. They may cost more to buy new than a comparable gas car, but as the miles pile on, there’s no need to worry about engine oil changes and emissions checks. Plus, cheap EVs are already here, with more to come in the near future.

While all of this is true, EVs aren’t exactly maintenance-free. There are still some things that need to be done to keep an electric car running like new for many years after it rolled off the assembly line.

There might not be an engine under the hood, and no manual or automatic transmission to worry about, but EVs still have transmissions, believe it or not. They also have brake fluid, brake pads, and coolant. And all of these—plus others—need attention over the course of a car’s life.

ERANGE EV tires are purpose-built for electric vehicles, combining efficiency, comfort and performance with advanced EcoPoint3 technology.

For this first installment of our new series on EV maintenance, I’ll focus on the Tesla Model 3, one of the best-selling electric models of all time, and a regular occurrence on roads everywhere in the United States, Europe, and beyond.

I’ll go through what maintenance is required by Tesla to keep the warranty intact, and also discuss items that are not part of the company’s service schedule but might still be worth considering for the long run.

The following list may seem a little too simple for someone who has switched from a gas or diesel car to an EV, but there’s no shortage of high-mileage electric cars out there, including countless Teslas, that are still going strong with minimal maintenance. Here’s what Tesla recommends owners look out for on the Model 3:

High-Efficiency Particulate (HEPA) filter and carbon filter replacement: every three years, for vehicles that have them from the factory

Similar to a combustion vehicle, the Tesla Model 3 uses brake fluid to push the brake pads onto the rotors. Brake fluid is hygroscopic, meaning it naturally absorbs moisture from the air. If there’s a lot of moisture contamination, hydraulic pressure drops, which leads to a softer brake pedal and longer braking distances. A brake fluid test reveals if it’s still good or if it needs replacing.

Even though all modern EVs use their electric motors to slow down, they still rely on mechanical brakes to increase safety, and the Model 3 is no different. To keep things running smoothly, Tesla recommends cleaning and lubricating the brake calipers, especially for cars that live in areas where the roads are salted during the winter.

The thickness of the brake pads also needs to be checked, though there have been plenty of cases out there of Tesla EVs with over 100,000 miles on the clock and the original brake pads still in good condition.

Yes, the Model 3 doesn’t have a hot engine, but it still needs a radiator to keep the thermal system running cool. Depending on where the car is located, debris can build up over time, reducing the radiator’s efficiency and limiting the car’s performance.

Tesla Model 3 windshield camera precision cleaning

Tesla’s advanced driver assistance systems rely on video cameras to react, but they can’t perform as intended if they’re obstructed. The company says that cleaning the inside of the windshield in the camera area is vital for clear visibility and optimal camera function.

To check if cleaning is required, owners can tap the Maintenance tab in the infotainment system.

EVs are known for being harder on tires than gas cars because acceleration and brake regeneration will put stress on the rubber. To prolong the life of a tire set, Tesla recommends rotating the tires every 6,250 miles.

This is also when you want to check the tires themselves. Because EVs often wear out tires quicker, it's important to keep an eye on tread depth. When it gets below 4/32nds of an inch, it's time to start looking for new tires. If your tread depth is below 2/32nds, replace them immediately.

If the driver notices vibrations in the steering wheel while driving, the wheels may need balancing. With unbalanced tires, handling, tire life, and steering components are affected.

If the vehicle pulls to one side when the steering wheel is straight, or if there’s uneven wear on the tires, a wheel alignment may be needed. The procedure is also recommended after installing new tires.

All of the vehicle’s maintenance needs can be viewed in the Maintenance Summary on the central touchscreen, which provides a record of when common actions were last performed and recommends when to perform them next.

Tesla says that all of these items need to be performed at an authorized service center. This includes servicing the low-voltage and high-voltage batteries. However, there are some maintenance actions that should be considered by owners who want to treat their EVs as their forever cars.

We’ve all heard of “lifetime fluids,” but ask any well-versed mechanic out there, and they’ll say that they don’t exist. Instead, car manufacturers refer to them when it’s their job to maintain the car under warranty. After the warranty expires, the owner is on the hook for all repairs, including those that could have been avoided.

The following recommendations are nowhere to be found in Tesla’s maintenance plan, but some technicians still recommend them. Even though they’re not required actions, Tesla has service procedures for all of them, and its service centers can perform them if the owner asks.

Tesla used to recommend changing the transmission fluid in its drive units every 100,000 miles, but that went the way of the dodo. Now, the company’s transmissions, which transfer power from the electric motor to the wheels, have built-in filters, but plenty of mechanics out there believe that it’s good practice to renew the fluid every 100,000 miles at the latest.

The Model 3 uses coolant to keep the high-voltage battery at an optimal temperature. Just like on a combustion car, the coolant needs to be checked and replaced if it becomes contaminated.

Over time, rubber bushes will lose their elasticity or even crack. If this happens, knocks or rattles will make their presence felt, requiring a visit to a service center. Even though Tesla implemented many manufacturing novelties over time, it still hasn’t figured out how to replace the age-old rubber bushes found in all cars.

Under warranty, Tesla's authorized service centers should handle all maintenance items. However, after the warranty expires, many of the maintenance actions found on this list can be easily done at home by the owner. Air filter changes and radiator cleaning are DIY jobs that shouldn't take hours to complete, even for people who haven't done any mechanical work before.

Best of all, though, Tesla has published all of its service manuals online, and anyone can follow the service procedures to do maintenance jobs. What's more, in recent years, plenty of independent EV shops have popped up, and they can usually handle repairs and maintenance at lower costs than Tesla. That said, Tesla's own shops will happily inspect and repair older models, too.

Keeping an EV on the road should be much cheaper than a gas car, but it still requires some maintenance. Over a five-year period, the main maintenance items should include at least one set of new tires, multiple tire rotations, two brake fluid tests and maybe one flush, two cabin air filter replacements, several brake checks, and at least one set of wiper blades.

#4415. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

#4414. Tesla Keeps Killing Cars. Now It Wants To Build Cybercabs In Germany

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla’s core lineup is shrinking as the company focuses in on robotaxis. Now, Tesla boss Elon Musk wants to take his autonomous vehicle manufacturing ambitions beyond Texas and begin Cybercab production in Germany.

The company plans to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory near Berlin, targeting production of up to one million Cybercabs. According to Reuters, Tesla intends to apply for permits before the end of the year, begin construction in the first half of 2027, and start German Cybercab production in 2029.

The news comes as Tesla keeps reducing the number of conventional cars on offer. Over the past year or so, it has retired entire models, dropped cheaper variants, and earmarked factory space for robots and robotaxis. Knowing that, the new German Cybercab plan starts to look less like an addition to Tesla’s business and more like a replacement for part of it.

The most significant departures this year were the Model S and Model X. Tesla ended both model lines and announced it would repurpose its former Fremont factory space to build Optimus humanoid robots. Granted, the S and X were aging, low-volume products, but they made Tesla look more like a traditional automaker.

The Cybertruck is next, although its departure has become a moving target. Musk initially announced a mid-2027 shutdown to free Texas factory space for Cybercabs, then extended production through the end of summer to fulfill its order backlog. But it’s still scheduled for retirement.

Not even the ubiquitous Model Y has escaped. Tesla dropped its cheapest all-wheel-drive version earlier this month, less than a year after introducing it. Buyers who want two motors must now stretch to the Premium AWD or just get the base rear-wheel-drive variant, which remains available.

Tesla isn’t abandoning human-driven cars altogether. The redesigned Roadster revealed last month is now promised for 2028, complete with thruster-assisted theatrics. After years of delays and a complete redesign, it’s still a vehicle Tesla promises to build.

Basically, the new Roadster offers spectacle, but it doesn’t fill the practical gaps left by a luxury sedan, a large SUV, and a pickup. Tesla doesn’t even seem to be interested in filling those gaps.

The Cybercab faces a different issue. Without manual controls, its usefulness depends on Tesla’s autonomous driving capabilities and permission to deploy them. In the U.S., regulators have already opened an investigation into how the vehicle complies with federal safety requirements. A German production facility doesn’t, by itself, settle where its output can operate.

Tesla’s struggle to get FSD approved in Europe shows how slow that process can be. Dutch regulators cleared the supervised system in April after more than 18 months of testing, but its rollout has since depended on individual countries granting permission. EU-wide approval remains pending, and Tesla has renamed it “Tesla Assisted Driving” and tightened its speed settings to address regulators’ concerns.

All that work is for software that still requires an attentive driver. Getting permission for a Cybercab with no steering wheel or pedals is a separate challenge. And now Tesla wants to build those in Europe…

Still, Tesla’s survival doesn’t only rest on the Cybercab. The Model 3 and Model Y are still very popular worldwide, and the Semi could give it a foothold in electric trucking. But shrinking its passenger car lineup while spending billions on robotaxis leaves Tesla with fewer alternatives if Musk’s driverless future takes longer or proves less profitable than he expects.

#4413. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#4412. Rimac Is Reportedly Ending Nevera Production After Selling Just 71 Cars

The electric hypercar set plenty of records, but it may have come in well under the purportedly planned production run of 190 examples.

Rimac is ending production of its all-electric Nevera hypercar at the end of 2026, Germany’s Auto Motor und Sport reports. And somewhat surprisingly, the same report suggests that just 71 of 190 planned Reveras were built over the course of its production run.

The base Nevera, and its later Nevera R variant, have held a number of records, including the title of world’s quickest car, what was once the EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and a quarter-mile run under 7.9 seconds. Those numbers may not have been enough to make the model a hit with buyers, though. According to the report, 51 of a planned 150 base-model Neveras were built, and 20 out of a planned 40 Nevera Rs reached production.

While the apparent final tally of Nevera production is striking, it is part of a larger pattern of electric hypercars failing to find an audience. The Lotus Evija once competed directly with Rimac’s Nevera, but Lotus has since moved on to a hybrid supercar with V-8 power. Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal-combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

See all results for Rimac Nevera for sale near 38654

Whether or not the Nevera itself was a success, the halo car did succeed in raising Rimac’s profile. Namesake founder Mate Rimac is now fully in charge of Bugatti, and Rimac Technology provides electric powertrain components to major cars like the Porsche 911 Turbo S. As the most significant electric hypercar to reach the market to date—well, perhaps along with the closely related Pininfarina Battista—the few Neveras in private hands represent a major leap forward for both electric performance and the Rimac brand itself.
