#4411. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#4410. Mercedes Is Bringing Hands-Free Driving To Certain U.S. Highways In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Mercedes is bringing a new suite of driver assistance features. The two big new ones are Mercedes' MB.Drive Assist Pro, an FSD-like system we recently tested, and Hands-Free Highway Assist.

Silly corporate naming conventions aside, this new system is impressive. MB.Drive Assist Pro is a true point-to-point system, capable of taking you from your starting point to your destination on its own in urban environments as long as you directly supervise it. Mercedes is still calling it an SAE Level 2 system, so you still need to pay attention, keep your hands on the wheel, and take over whenever it needs. But it can do the heavy lifting for you.

On the highway, the Hands-Free Highway Assist can completely take over inputs on approved roads at speeds up to 85 mph. You'll need radar cruise engaged to use it. Once it's on, though, it can change lanes, overtake slower vehicles, handle lane merging, and even take off-ramps for you on its own, assuming the conditions are appropriate. Think of it like Super Cruise, just from Mercedes.

"By bringing hands-free highway driving together with point-to-point assistance and expanding these technologies across our portfolio, we’re making them available to more customers across the U.S.," said Jason Hoff, CEO Mercedes-Benz North America. "That’s where sophisticated technology becomes meaningful: when it makes everyday driving more comfortable and convenient.”

China has already had the system, but Mercedes is going to begin bringing it to German and the U.S. The latter of which will actually get a sneak preview of it in December, 2026, but only in California. Select Californian customers will be able to participate in an Early Access Program (EAP), which will let them test out these new features. Only lessees of the 2026/2027 Mercedes CLA, 2027 GLC Electric SUV2, S-Class Sedan, GLE SUV and Coupe, and GLS will be eligible.

Rollout for the rest of the country will happen in Spring 2027, and it will be available for all Mercedes vehicles with the proper hardware equipped. Even owners of existing vehicles with the necessary hardware will be able to buy the feature and have it digitally installed via an over-the-air update.

#4408. Volkswagen prices its new ID. Cross for the UK, but the $35,000 version comes later

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

#4407. 10 Deltarune Moments That Feel Totally Different When You Replay Earlier Chapters

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Deltarune is a game that thrives not only on its narrative, but also on the individual mysteries set up by every cliffhanger and loose thread. As in any good story, major revelations have not only affected fans’ expectations for the future, but also their understanding of earlier events.

Thanks to fantastic use of irony and follow-through, some of the smallest moments in Deltarune’s earlier chapters have been completely recontextualized, and we’ll be talking about the wildest here.

As we wait for chapter 6, it’s important to lay out everything we know and everything that’s become clearer since the game’s initial demo release. They say hindsight is 20/20, so let’s see how it serves us going forward.

Ralsei’s recitation of the Prophecy is one of the first major setup moments in Deltarune, both as a fairly cliché story setup and a direct threat for the party to fight back against later. Since chapter 4, the Prophecy’s legitimacy and exact wording have been under heavy scrutiny.

Knowing that Ralsei knows everything destined to happen down to the minute details makes his narration and people-pleasing more unsettling than charming. Susie’s heavy relevance to the darkest parts of its story sets her romantic yearning for Noelle up as a major red flag, ripe for getting ripped down by the grimmer chapters to come.

Susie’s portion of the Prophecy is vague enough that it might not even be about her, whether that’s through a misstep by Ralsei or deliberate sabotage from an outside force. The Prophecy itself is far from set in stone, ironically, and subverting it is already becoming a major objective of the party.

This is a detailed and all purpose hub for Toby Fox's episodic Deltarune.

Throughout King’s fight at the tail end of the chapter, he spends most of his dialogue praising the Roaring Knight, assigning all his work and progress to their support. This was the very first mention we got of the Knight, and at the time most assumed they were some kind of fixture of the card kingdom.

We’ve gathered much more info on the Roaring Knight since, but King’s speech is the only case we have of them actually interacting with someone without hostility.

In every other appearance, they’ve been a snarling aggressor with cruel laughter as their only method of communication. Hearing that they not only aligned with King but inspired him does a lot for their threat, establishing them as more than just a beast.

The weird route was already unsettling enough when it dropped during Deltarune’s second chapter, adding a touch of that No Mercy dread Undertale was infamous for. Despite this, the route felt rather self-contained until chapter 4 gave players a chance to lock it in.

Now that chapter 5 has arrived and given us a massive follow-through, playing through chapter 2’s Weird Route feels even worse. Knowing how far it goes and seeing exactly what goes on to shatter Noelle’s psyche make the metanarrative pain hit all the harder.

Spamton’s Shadow Crystal fight is a massive tonal shift from the rest of the chapter on the main route, especially at the very end. The battle takes a lot of notes from Undertale’s Mettaton battles, with Spamton straight up taking on a form extremely similar to Mettaton NEO.

The actual text of the battle is all about Spamton trying to transcend his limits, which all sounds very familiar to anyone who has seen chapter 5’s Weird Route dialogue. Combined with the constant discussion of Heaven and his angelic design, Spamton’s fight feels very different from what we originally thought.

Angels specifically are feeling more and more relevant the longer the game goes, both to symbolize the player and the larger figures controlling the Prophecy. For a goofy salesman, Spamton feels far more relevant than ever expected.

As Deltarune's size and popularity only grows, many people wonder if they should play Undertale first, and they really should.

The Shelter, the massive bunker at the southernmost tip of Hometown’s map, has been mysterious since Deltarune’s very first chapter, with each release slowly giving us more and more details about it. Over time, we’ve learned plenty. It is likely the site of whatever terrible accident happened to Dess; multiple members of the town are acting to keep it sealed, and most recently, Kris has access to it.

Thanks to these facts, it is largely assumed to be some kind of central base for the Knight and whoever is assisting it in the Light World. This makes Kris’s access to it when they break our control all the more interesting. Kris is clearly willing to do something drastic, including working with those who directly oppose the party.

After the most recent reveal of the strange flower seeds Kris pocketed and likely took back to the bunker, it feels like we’re watching them teetering over a ledge with no way to help. If they’d even let us.

Tenna is a massive source of comedy in chapter 3, but he’s also the source of a very off-putting little tantrum towards the tail end of the chapter, right before his boss fight. In it, he laments not only the state of the Dreemurr family but specifically Kris, pointing out just how differently they’ve been acting over the course of the night.

We know that the source of this difference is the player’s interference, but that dichotomy is a major stress point, both for Kris and the player. Who knows what Kris really acts like and whether or not close friends like Susie, who met them after the swap, will actually care about them?

On our end, we really don’t know what Kris is capable of or what they’re willing to do when the chips are down, and it adds a layer of dread to the entire scene.

From Cooking, to the Rhythm game, and even Susiezilla, this is How To S-Rank All Minigames in Deltarune Chapter 3.

After all the buildup and vague hints towards the Knight, their sudden reveal in chapter 3 was a massive surprise, and the small amount of characterization we’ve gotten for them has painted a picture of their true motives.

Most interestingly, the scene that plays when you beat the Knight, where they seemingly knight Kris, has been given extra weight by how clearly Kris is standing in their corner. After fighting off the Flowers and pocketing the highly toxic seeds at the tail end of chapter 5, Kris is willing to go above and beyond, even considering harming themselves to align with the Knight’s goal.

This is a horrifying setup for what chapters 6 and 7 could bring, especially with 5 being marketed as “one last happy adventure.”

Working your way through Noelle’s house at the start of chapter 4 was a great peek into her psyche after not getting much for her in chapter 3, while also allowing us to put together a bit more info on Dess Holiday herself.

Not only did we get plenty of extra scenes between Susie and Noelle, but we also got some more direct moments to see how exactly Kris acts without the Soul piloting them, making it clear that they can survive without it, at least for limited periods.

Most importantly, finally meeting Hometown’s mayor, Carol Holiday, added a tension that immediately made her a candidate for the Knight to many players. I won’t say I fully buy that theory, but she is officially on the table as an incredibly potent threat, alluding to both knowledge of and cooperation with Kris’s goal.

Chapter 4’s dark world was shockingly somber at times, setting a future tone while finalizing quite a few rules for how light world monsters and Darkners can overlap. Namely, through Gerson’s inclusion, we learned that dead Darkners, at least monsters, can manifest in Dark Worlds if items with their dust are within a fountain’s range.

This opens the door for any missing or dead characters to potentially show up in the future, or for items connected deeply to certain characters to manifest either as them or similarly to them. I fully believe this is how we’ll get some extra context on Rudy after his “falling down” early in chapter 5, and that it will lead to massive drama going forward.

From the earliest launch of Deltarune, fans have assumed the strange voice that speaks to us during the character creator was Gaster, based on the speech pattern that it uses and the dialogue from the Deltarune Twitter.

Following his extra dialogue in chapters 3 and 4, I grew extremely confident in that theory, and facts from both the normal and Weird Routes of chapter 5 have fully convinced me that we will meet the Man Who Speaks in Hands before Deltarune is through. Given what happens to Onionsan via one of Gaster’s Goners and his clear significance in the “B-Side” cutscene in the Weird Route, he is by far our biggest mystery and one that fully recontextualizes every bit of dialogue we get from him.

Deltarune chapter 5 is, unsurprisingly, full of mysteries players are still trying to get their heads around.

#4406. The Electric Baby Land Rover Defender And Range Rover GT Will Begin Production Next Year

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

JLR's all-electric baby Defender is coming soon. According to Car and Driver, JLR boss PB Balaji recently said on an earnings call that the smaller, all-electric Defender will go into production at the end next year, alongside the upcoming Range Rover GT. There's no official name for the bite-sized Defender, but Balaji reportedly didn't want to call it the Defender Sport.

While JLR didn't give much info on what the electric baby Defender will be, we do know that it will be built on the same Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA) platform that underpins the Range Rover GT. So it makes sense that it'll be built at the same factory. That factory currently builds the existing piston-powered Discovery Sport and the Range Rover Evoque. So JLR is basically just replacing the current combustion cars with their new electric counterparts.

Despite both cars being built in the same factory, Balaji seemed to suggest that only the Defender will go into production in 2027. There's not much word on any technical specs just yet, but EMA supports 800-volt architectures and is capable of housing both pure battery-electric powertrains and hybrids. The baby Defender could very well offer both, but whichever powertrain it has, it'll need to be capable off-road to deliver on its name.

According to Motor1, Mark Cameron, managing director of Defender and Discovery brands, said "We have got to make sure everything we do as Defender has the DNA of the brand: epic built-to-last, go-anywhere capability."

Pricing, specs, and range are all still under wraps, although it might make sense for either new electric product to have the same 118.5-kWh battery as the current Range Rover Electric. With it, the electric Rover is capable of 333 miles of range, and that uses a conventional platform. The battery is also capable of 350 kW DC fast-charging, which would be very competitive in the segment, so it might make sense for JLR to roll with that battery tech. The big Range Rover Electric has a dual-motor powertrain, with 542 horsepower, but that might be a bit much for a baby Defender. Although, there could be a go-fast version with that much power, similar to the current Defender Octa.

Land Rover pushed the current full-size Defender's electric replacement out to sometime in the 2030s, so there shouldn't be any confusion between the full-size and bite-size models. If production begins in late 2027, that means we could see the baby Defender soon.

#4405. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#4404. 2027 Acura Integra Type S

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 32712

The Acura Integra Type S is the swankier cousin of the boy-racer Honda Civic Type R. The two share their mechanical underpinnings and hatchback body style, but the Acura is dressed in a more respectable-looking outfit. A lusty 320-hp turbocharged inline-four is under the hood and mates exclusively to a six-speed manual transmission. The combination loves to spin its front tires excitedly, and it's a riot to drive.

An expertly tuned chassis gives the Integra Type S high-spirited handling, and it rides comfortably enough for long trips. The engineers responsible for this gem had driving enthusiasts in mind when this Acura was planned. The cabin is slightly upscale from the Civic Type-R as well, although not as much as you’d think given the six grand price delta between the two.

Expert Tip: Its premium badge and $ 56,000 price tag put the Integra Type S into contention with some European rivals that offer richer accommodations.

Compare the 2027 Acura Integra Type S with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

Acura has added a limited-production Heritage Edition to the lineup for 2027. Only 700 will be offered in the U.S., all painted Blazing Phoenix Yellow and wearing special copper-colored aluminum wheels. The Heritage Edition is also emblazoned with black exterior badging and features a titanium shift knob.

The standard Integra Type S gets a few changes for the 2027 model year, too, including new gloss black wheels, yellow brake calipers, dark gray interior trim, and gloss black climate control knobs. Several features have been added as standard, such as memory settings for the driver’s seat and an exterior mirror tilt-down feature that can be set to automatically dip the mirrors when you shift into reverse.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

A 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four with 310 pound-feet of torque is the sole engine for the Integra Type S. Like the Civic Type R, the Integra Type S routes the power exclusively through a six-speed manual transmission and front-wheel drive with a limited-slip differential. Shifter action is wonderfully light and precise—this is one of the best manual shifters in the business—and clutch take-up is smooth and intuitive. With all 310 pound-feet of torque available at 2600 rpm, you could skip a shift or two without worry, but it'd be a shame to miss out on all the fun.

Objectively, roadholding and braking match the Civic Type R, with the Integra Type S pulling 1.02 g's on the skid pad and stopping from 70 mph in just 153 feet. Subjectively, the Civic feels ever so slightly more vivacious from behind the wheel. The Integra Type S knows how to chill in less demanding situations, slipping into an almost-calm cruising mode. All Type S models come with 19-inch wheels wearing summer tires, Brembo brakes, and an exhaust system with three center-mounted exhaust pipes.

In Comparison: The Integra Type S's brisk 60-mph sprint time is nearly two seconds quicker than the 7.0-second time we posted with the standard six-speed Integra and just 0.2 seconds behind the last Civic Type R we tested.

The EPA estimates that the Integra Type S will deliver 21 mpg city, 28 mpg highway, and 24 mpg combined. It's also worth noting the Type S returned an impressive 31 mpg on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, three miles per gallon better than its EPA rating. For more information about the Integra Type S's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

In Comparison: The Audi S3 is slightly more efficient, earning EPA estimates of 23 mpg city and 31 mpg highway, as is the BMW M235 Gran Coupe with estimates of 24 mpg city and 33 mpg highway.

First Row: Acura plays the long game with the Type S's interior, favoring conservative design and quality materials over outright flash. There are plenty of parts shared with the Honda Civic under the skin, but Acura pulls styling elements from its SUVs to foster the familial vibe. Distinctive features include mildly bolstered sport seats upholstered with perforated, faux-suede fabric, “Type S” embossed headrests, and subtle touches including a Type S shift knob, boot, and steering wheel emblem.

Second Row: A pair of individual rear bucket seats and a small center console armrest replace the standard Integra's rear bench. There's room for two in back, but the lack of features such as rear air vents and seat heaters is a notable omission in a supposedly premium car.

Cargo Capacity: Thanks to its Civic roots, the Integra Type S offers the same 24 cubic feet of cargo room accessed via a large hatchback. We fit five carry-on suitcases in the trunk and managed to squeeze in a total of 18 with the rear seats folded.

The Type S gets the same 10.2-inch digital gauge cluster as the rest of the Integra lineup; a 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is standard. A wireless smartphone charging pad, a head-up display, and a pair of USB ports are also included. All versions come with a top-tier 16-speaker, 530-watt ELS Studio 3D premium audio system.

A host of driver-assistance features are included as standard in the Integra Type S, including automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane-keeping assist, and adaptive cruise control.

For information about the Integra Type S's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Acura offers a longer powertrain warranty than most of its competitors, with powertrain coverage stretching up to six years or 70,000 miles. Complimentary scheduled maintenance is also included, unlike the Audi S3 or the Mercedes-Benz CLA-Class.

#4403. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

Thanks for that and now I have a place to send a friend who wants to buy a Tesla with FSD and thinks he'll never have to watch the road.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#4402. Stellantis Reappoints Broderdorf, Promotes Kuniskis in CEO Shuffle

Bob Broderdorf is returning from medical leave to lead Dodge, while Tim Kuniskis is taking over as Stellantis’s U.S. chief commercial officer.

Stellantis is playing another round of musical chairs with its executive team. This time, most of the changes stem from Bob Broderdorf’s return to the company. Broderdorf took medical leave from his position as Jeep’s CEO in August. He was replaced by Branden Coté, who retains his position as head of Jeep.

When Broderdorf’s departure from Jeep was announced, Stellantis had said he would come back in a different leadership role. Now off medical leave, Broderdorf will return to CEO status, this time as head of Dodge.

See all results for used cars for sale near 63129

This isn’t Broderdorf’s first time at Dodge. He’s held seven different positions related to marketing, sales, product planning, and operations throughout his 25-year tenure at Stellantis. Dodge has been led by Matt McAlear since 2024, but McAlear has been spread thin at Stellantis since February, when he took over as Chrysler’s CEO and head of Alfa Romeo North America. McAleer will now focus solely on Chrysler, which is expected to release three new models in the next few years.

Chrysler’s lineup currently consists of just the Pacifica minivan. However, the brand has already announced the Airflow, a new compact SUV slated to launch in 2028 and start at less than $40,000, and is also working on the Arrow and Arrow Cross, which will come in under $30,000.Both CEOs will report to Tim Kuniskis, who assumes a new role as U.S. chief commercial officer. Kuniskis joined Stellantis in 1992 and served in several leadership roles before retiring from his position as head of Dodge and Ram in May 2024.

Retirement only lasted about seven months, though, and Kuniskis reportedly said he was “bored to death” after about two weeks out of work. By December 2024, Stellantis had announced Kuniskis’s appointment as Ram’s CEO. Since his return, Kuniskis has passed the Ram brand to Matt VanDyke and has taken over as head of American Brands, North America Marketing, SRT, and Stellantis’s Direct Connection parts division.

Now, Kuniskis adds U.S. retail, fleet sales, and the dealer network to his long list of leadership divisions following the departure of Michael Orange, former senior vice president of U.S. sales and network performance. Kuniskis will report to Stellantis North America’s chief operating officer, Pablo Di Si, who was appointed to the role earlier this month.

Di Si said in a press release that the leadership moves create a “clear line of decision-making” across the organization, which he says is important as Stellantis works to reach targets outlined in its FaSTLAne 2030 growth plan.

#4400. 2028 Ford Mustang Cobra with a Race Car-Derived V-8 Is Worth Waiting For

The Cobra finally returns to the Mustang lineup and essentially resumes the track-focused role last held by the Shelby GT350.

Ford only just launched the Mustang Dark Horse SC earlier this year, but the Blue Oval brand isn’t letting up when it comes to high-performance versions of its iconic pony car. While the S650-generation Mustang introduced the new Dark Horse branding—at the expense of the legendary Shelby nameplate—and saw the arrival of the new $300,000-plus GTD, Ford’s upcoming Mustang variant revives a famous name from the past: Cobra. The new Mustang Cobra is expected to slot between the Dark Horse and Dark Horse SC as an indirect successor to the last Shelby GT350, providing track-ready performance and high-fidelity driver engagement.

The Shelby GT350, offered from 2015–2020, is considered one of the best Mustangs ever, thanks to its naturally aspirated flat-plane-crank 5.2-liter V-8 known as Voodoo. The last Cobra is also coveted by Mustang fans, so the new track-focused model has big shoes to fill. And with a new engine most likely under the Cobra’s hood, there’s potential for another legendary Mustang to be born.

See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang for sale near 12020

The Cobra will continue to utilize the S650 platform, itself an evolution of the S550 chassis that underpinned the Mustang from 2015–2023. The Cobra will adapt the Mustang into a dedicated track car, and we think it will also spawn a more hardcore Cobra R with even more extreme aerodynamics, stronger brakes, and greater weight savings, potentially even removing the backseat. We expect the Cobra’s bodywork to be based on the Dark Horse SC, but with small tweaks and possibly a rear wing that harkens back to the 2000 Cobra R.

Mustang fans are obviously clamoring for the return of the Voodoo, but we don’t think that’s what Ford has in store. Fret not, however, because the automaker is cooking up something special for the new Cobra.

Instead of the 5.2-liter Voodoo, the new Cobra will pack a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter engine derived from the Mustang GT3 race car that has triumphed at the 24 Hours of Daytona and secured a podium at Le Mans. The Coyote-based GT3 engine features a cross-plane crank, but the teaser video released by Ford emitted a high-revving scream, so there’s a chance that the Cobra’s engine will switch to a flat-plane-crank setup. Still, if you’ve recently been to an IMSA race, you’ll know the GT3 car produces a thunderous soundtrack, so enthusiasts are in for an auditory treat regardless.

Although Ford hasn’t confirmed that the Cobra will adapt the GT3 race car’s engine, in the first teaser it said the car would pack a “heart born from racing.” We don’t expect the Cobra to come close to the Dark Horse SC or GTD in terms of power, but we wouldn’t be shocked if the 5.4-liter V-8 exceeds the 550 horsepower that the GT3 car is restricted to by racing regulations.

See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang for sale near 12020

Better yet, the new 5.4-liter V-8 will be paired with a six-speed manual for maximum driver engagement. We think Ford will likely employ the Tremec TR-3160 transmission already used in the Dark Horse.

At the moment, the Mustang has the V-8 muscle car world all to itself. Dodge is expected to stuff a supercharged V-8 back into the Charger for the 2028 model year, while Chevy is gearing up to bring back the Camaro around 2028. The only other V-8-powered car under $100,000 is the Corvette, which has a completely different form factor with its mid-engine layout, but it will likely still be cross-shopped against the Cobra.

Pricing is probably the biggest risk. Ford needs to make sure it doesn’t alienate its customers by making it too expensive, given that the Dark Horse SC already has a hefty $105,585 asking price (about $20K more than the GT500 that it replaced). The new 5.4-liter V-8 will also have to make a strong impression as a successor to the much-loved Voodoo.

The Mustang Cobra will likely be revealed in early 2027 and go on sale before the end of the year. We expect pricing to start somewhere in the $80,000 range, but it could easily climb to $100,000 for a Cobra R model.

#4399. 10 Open-World Games You Can Finish in 10 Hours & Under

Elena Chapella is a Writer for DualShockers. Previously an award-winning journalist, Elena is passionate about writing what she loves.

When any gamer hears about open world games, they immediately (safely) assume that the game would proceed to take hours upon hours to complete. However, that’s not always the case with open world games.

In fact, some of these games can be completed in less than 10 hours.

If you enjoy exploration-focused titles that are free of filler, we recommend the ten fastest open-world games to 100%.

For players who are wanting a one-and-done experience with an open world game, being able to beat it within the same day or two days maximum, these games scratch that itch. You’re able to hop in and complete the game practically quicker than you can download it, and it’s just the right amount of content to tide you over until the next game.

While others are diving into open world games to sink hundreds upon hundreds of hours into them, you can rest assured that these games won’t eat up your schedule.

The thing about Outer Wilds is that the world itself is the final boss, with players only having a limited amount of time in order to save the universe – but it’s not done on its own. The game’s DLC, Echoes of the Eye, is about 10 and half hours long, obviously shorter for faster players.

The DLC doesn’t replace anything in the game, but it’s rather a separate and self-contained location, more than ready for players to dive in and unravel its secrets. This way, if players are wanting a taste of Outer Wilds without going through the whole game, they can easily do so.

This is especially the case if you’ve already beaten the game/solved the mystery of the main story. Since there isn’t really any replayability, the DLC offers a whole new mystery altogether – in a way, it’s like you’re playing the game for the first time all over again, and it can be solved pretty quickly.

Thankfully, there are also even more DLCs if you want more mystery, but they aren’t anywhere near as condensed as Echoes of the Eye.

There’s something particularly special about Shadow of the Colossus: the game is labelled as an open world, but many players would walk away from it thinking that it’s a semi-open world due to just how empty the world itself is.

Of course, that’s typically a bad thing for open worlds, but the unique thing about Shadow of the Colossus is that it would not work without that emptiness. Combine this with a linear order for the bosses themselves (which are platforming puzzles as well), a vague yet compelling story and a genuinely cool premise, and you’ve got a game that’s as fun as it is challenging.

One of my students refers to the game as “Rated T for Teen Mario,” and I'm bound to agree, if that helps get the idea across. And just like Mario, the game can be beaten pretty quickly: about 7 hours, in fact.

With that in mind, if this is a game that interests you, be prepared to spend most of those 7 hours climbing rather than fighting; you’re going to love it regardless.

Right now, The Legend of Zelda once again has the gaming community in a complete buzz thanks to the fantastic reception to the Ocarina of Time Remake.

The series is continuously revolutionary, constantly evolving and redefining the open world genre as we know it. However, many tend to forget that open world Zelda didn’t start with Breath of the Wild, it started with the very first entry in the entire franchise.

The nice part about the game is that it’s not long at all (especially when compared to its sequels that will come over the next few decades) – averaging only at about 8 hours to beat the game. Players who want a traditional Zelda experience in a short amount of time can’t find any other game that would be a better fit.

And as the game comes up on its 40th anniversary, it’s all the more reason to dive into where it all began.

Obviously, both Red Dead Redemption games are massive, telling all kinds of stories jam-packed in a rich world of historical fiction, so it would take a while to beat either entry. However, the first game’s DLC, Undead Nightmare, is a fantastic stand-alone story that only takes about 6 and a half hours to complete.

Undead Nightmare takes everything you love about the classic Red Dead Redemption, but with a twist: suddenly, everyone is trying to survive a zombie apocalypse that came about practically overnight. The world and everything you can do within it, naturally, is related to this instead of your standard robberies and bounties.

Since the world is so condensed, the DLC goes by much quicker than most, but it’s an absolute blast from start to finish. In fact, it’s widely considered to be one of the greatest DLCs of all time, simply for how refreshingly unique and fun it is.

With that in mind, the fact that this game can be completed quicker than a standard work shift just makes it all the better.

Of all the Assassin's Creed games, the shortest mainline entry (non-DLC game) is easily Assassin's Creed: Rogue, clocking in at about 11 hours to be beaten (again, it’s much quicker than that for veteran AC fans and seasoned gamers as a whole).

Surprisingly, the game has one of the more unique stories that the series has seen, focusing on an Assassin named Shay Patrick Cormac literally going rogue, slaughtering the brotherhood he knows and siding with the Templars.

And the best part of the story is the fact that the modern-day segments are thankfully incredibly short – the segments that drag and feel like a chore in all the other titles in the franchise don’t bog down this game.

Overall, it’s the perfect bite-sized game for Assassin’s Creed content, regardless of if you’re a fan or even brand new to the series. It’s truly one of a kind, especially for a series like AC.

From the titans of Xenoblade to the lawns of Santa Destroy, these Wii open-world games prove curiosity always pays off if you’re willing to get lost.

If you were given 10 hours to simply explore New York City and soak it all in, you wouldn’t even be an eighth of the way through your journey before you reach that time. The fact that Marvel's Spider-Man brought in NYC on a similar (still scaled down) scale cemented the game’s timeframe as you continue to whip around as The Friendly Neighborhood himself.

Yet, you don’t have anywhere near as many superhero duties in Spider-Man: Miles Morales, so obviously, it will take you a lot less time. It would take about 8 hours, in fact.

Since you’re playing the game as Miles Morales (duh) while Peter Parker is still around and kicking, you’re basically a superhero in training. This training will have you busy constantly taking down bad guys and saving the day, serving as the sole Spider-Man in NYC for several hours until Peter comes back from vacation with MJ.

Or you could just swing around New York City doing whatever you want for that timeframe, you’d get the same amount of enjoyment.

Just because a game is a horror game doesn’t mean it can’t also be open world, and in DREDGE, our open world is a vast, dangerous ocean. Even then, it’s nowhere near as dangerous as it will be once your sanity drains due to the Lovecraftian terrors you’ll encounter.

It sounds horrifying, but it’s actually the coziest fishing game you’d ever imagine. You fish, fill out your encyclopedia, discover aberrations with the marine life and upgrade your ship, but the real fun comes from the simplest mechanic: sorting the fish into your boat. Seriously, the inventory management is the most addictive part of the whole game.

The nice part is that it’s wrapped up quickly, too, taking only about 9 and a half hours to complete – but trust me, you’re going to willingly sink far more hours into the game (and your ship). And if that doesn’t sound like enough content in the game for how much I sing its praises, it also has two equally dense and fun DLCs.

When it comes to short, yet full open world games, you cannot get any better of an experience than with DREDGE.

The lovely thing about Eastshade isn’t just how stunning of a game it is, but also the fact that it can be beaten pretty quickly and pretty easily – just around 9 hours.

The whole game is about finding the most beautiful spots in the game to paint them (using a photography mechanic), so those entire 9 hours are filled with genuine beauty. Of course, since it’s open world, there are side quests (artwork commissions) and other things to do, but you’re going to be far more caught up in how pretty the world is.

And for those who love subtle, environmental storytelling, this world is full of it. You can learn more while you’re out and about exploring in it, or from the various other characters that you can talk to.

It’s one of the few open world games that keeps you busy without actively stressing you out; since, after all, the point of the game is to relax you, you’re going to find yourself in a comfortable state of bliss while playing.

If you’ve ever wanted to feel like you’re driving a pod around Tatooine (like any Star Wars fan would), you would have a fantastic time with Sable.

The game seems pretty surface-level and simple: just ride around on your sand-speeder and enjoy the game’s lovely art style, but once you start playing, you’ll see it’s a lot deeper than you’d expect. It’s supposed to be about the protagonist’s self-discovery on their home planet, but by the end of your adventure, you’re going to feel like you’ve gone on a self-discovery of your own.

While the game can be completed in about 7 and a half hours, it’s actually better if you take your time with the exploration – that’s the game’s strongest component, after all. Why not take the time to enjoy a world as pretty and interesting as this one?

It’s not perfectly polished; it’s actually pretty janky of a game at times, but if anything, it makes you love the game and all the charm it has even more. At the same time, if some of the previously mentioned jank (charm) is a little too much, then rest assured that you can get through this game very, very quickly.

A Short Hike is just that: short. It’s not the kind of short where it’s on the shorter end of a long game, no, the game is only about an hour and a half long. If you try to complete every single element within it to 100% the game, you’re looking at about 4 hours, an incredibly tiny open world game.

The premise of the game is simple: you’re hiking up a mountain. If you run into anyone or anything on the way there, you’re more than welcome to interact with them, but it’s optional if you’re wanting to just get to the top. Considering how short the game is, I’d recommend not skipping anything if you can help it, just to get the richest experience you can.

Don’t rush through this hike, either. The game is already short enough, and there is so much enjoyable content that you don’t want to miss out on while on the way to the top.

But as we’ve learned with games like these: it’s not about the destination, it’s about the journey, so don’t be afraid to go on that journey.

Our picks for 10 open-world games that won't leave you feeling burned out from exploring only a few hours into them.

#4396. Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.

Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health

Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans

The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

#4395. Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a new production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:

If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

#4393. BYD is bringing its $10,000 ‘Great’ Seagull overseas, but it won’t replace the Dolphin Surf

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

In China, the new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

The second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the new version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The new setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

The current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).
