#4376. 10 Survival Games That Don’t Make Hunger Their Whole Personality

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

Survival games have had a hold on me for years now. There’s truly nothing like crash-landing somewhere hostile with nothing but the clothes on your back, punching a tree, and slowly building something that resembles a home. What I could absolutely do without, though, is the little drumstick icon that starts flashing at me roughly ten minutes into every new world.

From Rain World's terrifying sights to Subnautica's oceanic survival, these are the 10 Best Open World Survival Games.

Look, I get it. Hunger is realistic, and in some games, it genuinely adds to the experience. But far too often, it feels like a chore that’s been bolted on because that’s just what survival games do, and I’m not being funny, but I didn’t plan an entire expedition just to turn around because my character fancies a snack.

Thankfully, not every developer feels the same way. Some have turned food into a reward rather than a punishment, some have made hunger completely optional, and a few have decided that your character doesn’t need to eat at all. They’re all still survival games, and some of them are pretty brutal, so let’s take a look at my favourites that found far more interesting ways to try and kill you.

Valheim is pretty much the poster child for survival games that do food differently. There’s no hunger meter, and you will never starve to death, no matter how long you go without eating. Instead, you can have up to three different foods active at once, with each of them boosting your maximum health and stamina before slowly wearing off.

Skipping a meal won’t hurt you, but it will leave you with a measly 25 health and 50 stamina, healing a single hit point every ten seconds. Considering a single troll can flatten you in a matter of seconds, that’s more than enough motivation to get cooking. Food becomes part of your preparation, just like repairing your gear before a big boss fight, rather than something you need to do just to stay alive.

Note: Iron Gate reworked the entire food system with the Hearth & Home update back in 2021, and truth be told, not everyone was thrilled about it at the time.

After more than five years in Early Access and over 17 million copies sold, Valheim finally hit 1.0 on 9 September 2026, together with the Deep North biome. Eating is still optional. Heading into the Mistlands on an empty stomach, however, is a mistake you’ll only make once.

Keen Games, the Frankfurt studio behind Portal Knights, didn’t exactly hide where its inspiration came from. Ahead of Early Access, the team said that Enshrouded would have no hunger meter, no thirst meter and no sleep meter, and that Valheim was the closest comparison for how food would work. And honestly? It shows, in the best possible way.

Food in Enshrouded is all about buffs. You get three food slots, and only one food of each type can be active at a time, which nudges you towards mixing and matching rather than just shovelling roasted meat into your mouth. Some meals boost your health, others your melee or magic damage, and it ends up feeling much more like putting together an RPG build than ticking off a survival chore.

Note: About six months into Early Access, Keen Games added an optional Survival difficulty that brings the hunger bar back. On that setting, it can actually kill you.

I think that’s the perfect compromise. If you want the classic experience, it’s there for you, but if you don’t, you’ll never have to think about it. More than five million players had already wandered into Embervale before the 1.0 release on 15 October 2026, so I’m clearly not the only one who appreciates that.

Terraria has never had a hunger meter. Sure, food exists, but it gives you the Well Fed buff, a lovely little boost to your stats rather than something standing between you and certain death. You can spend hundreds of hours digging, building and taking down bosses without ever having to think about lunch.

That changed, sort of, with the 1.4.3 update. Re-Logic teamed up with Klei Entertainment for a crossover with Don’t Starve Together, and the result was The Constant, a secret world seed that brings in hunger, Don’t Starve-style shading and darkness that actively hurts you. Hunger works in stages, and if you ignore it for long enough, you will start starving.

Note: The whole crossover started with a Reddit AMA for Terraria’s 10th anniversary, where the team said Don’t Starve Together was the franchise they’d most like to collaborate with. Klei just so happened to be reading.

I absolutely love this approach. Nobody is forced into it, but it’s there as an opt-in challenge for anyone who wants it. The fact that you need to type in a secret seed to even get hunger tells you everything you need to know about how essential it is to the Terraria experience.

Players will need to be extra careful when exploring in these open-world and survival games.

Astroneer has a pretty simple take on survival: you need oxygen, and that’s about it. Your shelter provides you with both power and oxygen, so as long as you stay within range, you’re absolutely fine. The moment you wander off, though, your meter starts to drop, which is where tethers come in to carry that oxygen with you.

What I love is how that one mechanic shapes everything else. Your tether lines double as breadcrumbs, so you always have a way back home, and the tension only really kicks in when you’re deep in a cave and very much off the grid. It’s survival with all of the tension and none of the snack breaks, and that’s exactly why I keep going back to it.

System Era Softworks released Astroneer into Early Access in December 2016, before launching the full game in February 2019. Sadly, co-founder and lead artist Paul Pepera passed away in March 2017, before the game was finished. His distinctive low-poly style still defines Astroneer to this day, and by March 2022, the game had been purchased nearly four million times.

No Man’s Sky doesn’t have a hunger meter, a thirst meter or anything that even resembles sleep. What it does have is life support and hazard protection, and both of those need topping up whilst you explore planets that are, more often than not, actively trying to kill you. Some players will argue those are just hunger and thirst with different names, and fair enough, but in practice it feels completely different.

You’re not foraging for berries. You’re mining oxygen and sodium, refining resources and keeping your exosuit running whilst dodging toxic rain or extreme temperatures. Instead of pulling you away from exploring, your survival is tied directly into it.

Food did eventually find its way into the game with a full cooking system, letting you turn ingredients into dishes that restore life support or hazard protection. There’s even a food critic, Cronus, who will rate your culinary creations and reward you with nanites. It’s completely optional, slightly absurd and exactly the kind of thing No Man’s Sky does best.

Subnautica does have hunger and thirst in its default Survival mode, so this one comes with a little asterisk. When you start a new game, though, you can pick Freedom mode instead, which is identical to Survival, just without hunger and thirst. You’ll still have to manage your oxygen, your health and your nerves, and trust me, that is more than enough.

Plenty of players recommend Freedom as the best way to experience Subnautica for the first time, and I’d have to agree. Inventory space is already tight, and every slot you don’t fill with fish is a slot you can use for resources. That way, you can fully focus on exploring the oceans of planet 4546B, which are, quite frankly, terrifying enough on their own.

Note: Freedom mode isn’t a late addition, either. It has been there almost from the start, and PC Gamer’s preview in January 2015, just weeks into Early Access, already listed it alongside Survival.

Unknown Worlds launched the full game on 23 January 2018, celebrating with a livestream from the Monterey Bay Aquarium. By then, nearly two million people already owned it. Considering what lurks in the deeper parts of Subnautica, I personally would’ve picked a slightly less fishy location.

These games are sure to keep fans of the Subnautica series entertained.

Satisfactory is a factory-building game first and a survival game a very distant second, but it still drops you onto an alien planet full of wildlife that would love nothing more than to take a bite out of you. What it doesn’t do is make you eat. Food is purely there to heal you, and the planet’s edible flora are more like a first aid kit than an actual meal.

Paleberries heal 10 HP, Beryl Nuts a little less, and the Bacon Agaric mushroom heals 20. Eventually, you can even process them into inhalers, because of course the answer to everything in Satisfactory is automation. The only real hunger in this game is your factory’s endless appetite for more power, more iron and more conveyor belts.

Note: ADA, your ever-so-helpful AI companion, refers to the Bacon Agaric as Amanita Lardum. Whether it actually tastes like bacon remains a mystery.

Coffee Stain Studios released Satisfactory 1.0 on 10 September 2024, after over five years in Early Access and 5.5 million copies sold. And the big reveal in the release date trailer? A flushable toilet. We all have our priorities.

Starbound, Chucklefish’s sci-fi sandbox, lets you decide on your relationship with food right at character creation. Casual mode removes the need to eat entirely, Survival mode adds a hunger meter, and Hardcore combines hunger with permadeath for anyone who enjoys suffering. There’s no switching later on, so you’d better know what you want before you start.

Interestingly, hunger had actually been taken out during development, and was only brought back for the 1.0 release on 22 July 2016, specifically for the Survival and Hardcore modes. In those, food rots over time, and you will starve if you ignore it. In Casual, food still heals you and grants buffs, so cooking never feels pointless.

I really appreciate a game that respects the fact that some of us just want to build a pretty space station and go planet-hopping in peace. Not every adventure needs a ration plan. Starbound can still be pretty challenging in other ways, but in Casual mode, the biggest threat on a new planet is the local wildlife, not your rumbling stomach.

There are so many great co-op games coming out today, and many allow players to just explore and relax together.

Pacific Drive is a survival game where you don’t need to eat, drink or sleep. Instead, almost all of the survival pressure lands squarely on your station wagon. You patch up panels, swap out tyres, keep the battery charged and the tank full, all whilst driving through the bizarre, anomaly-filled Olympic Exclusion Zone.

Seth Rosen, who led the game’s design, has been pretty open about the fact that a lot of his choices were aimed at smoothing out the things that bugged him about survival games. He even had pages of notes on turning radiation damage into an exposure meter, but ultimately decided against it, since you already have your hands full taking care of the car without another time pressure and distraction. As Rosen put it, the car’s health is generally a better indicator of how a run is going than your own.

Note: Creative director and CEO Cassandra Dracott’s 1989 Buick Estate was the primary reference car during early development. Her parents’ Volvo station wagon, which became the car she drove from the moment she could drive, played a part, too.

Ironwood Studios released Pacific Drive on 22 February 2024, and it sold over a million copies within a year. There’s even a television adaptation in development, and I truly have no idea how they’re planning to make a car the main character. I cannot wait to find out.

LEGO Fortnite launched on 7 December 2023 with a fairly traditional hunger system. You could already switch it off when creating a world, but for anyone who kept it on, it wasn’t exactly a great time. Within two weeks, Epic patched it to make snacks more filling, because food simply wasn’t reducing hunger by enough. In hindsight, it was the first sign that hunger and LEGO minifigures weren’t the most natural pairing.

In mid-2024, Epic added Cozy mode, which turned hunger, temperature and stamina off by default. That should’ve been the end of it, but Epic eventually went one step further and removed hunger from Odyssey altogether. Food and potions still exist and give you buffs, but there’s no meter to keep topped up anymore.

Note: Not everyone was happy about it, with some players saying the change made the game feel a little too arcade-like.

Personally, I think it was the right call for a game that lives inside Fortnite and attracts plenty of younger and newer players. Odyssey is all about building villages, exploring and fighting off the occasional Storm-Wild creature. Nobody needed to stop every few minutes to hunt down yet another LEGO berry.

These survival games are the best to come back to and explore to your heart's content solo or with friends time and time again.

#4375. The New Smaller Land Rover Defender Will Arrive First as an EV

Likely called the Defender Sport, this electric downsized Defender will ride on the same platform as the Range Rover GT.

At Jaguar Land Rover, the word Sport essentially means “fun size.” Full-size Range Rover? That’s just a Range Rover. The wee version that’s a bit nippier through the bends? That’ll be the Range Rover Sport. Now, with the Defender getting its own scaled-down Sport version, it’s going to be electric.

Now, there’s still a chance that this smaller Defender model could be named something other than Sport, as JLR head PB Balaji has been a little cagey about explicitly calling the upcoming car Defender Sport. Speaking on JLR’s second earnings call, he confirmed that the factory that currently builds the Discovery Sport and Evoque will be manufacturing the new Defender and the Range Rover GT starting next year.

See all results for Land Rover Defender Sport for sale near 53206

The two cars will share JLR’s new Electrified Modular Architecture platform, which is designed to support 800-volt electric vehicles and also hybrids. However, Balaji indicated that only the battery-electric small Defender would be ready to go by the end of next year.

Pretty much everything in JLR’s range (leaving out the rebooting Jaguar brand) has pretty impressive off-road chops, but a Defender Sport has to be particularly special. It’s one thing to offer a smaller, more agile Range Rover Sport that has most of the luxury of the full-size vehicle with better agility. This new model will be the first in a planned series of vehicles that will establish Defender not just as a single product but as a brand.

JLR probably can’t get away with how Ford positions the Bronco and the Bronco Sport as a Jeep Wrangler competitor and an Escape crossover, respectively, with more personality. The Defender Sport might be smaller than its big brother, but it’s going to need to offer up most of the same off-road chops.

As distinct from the electric version of the Mercedes-Benz G-class, which tucked its batteries onboard in such a way as to offer up all of the same ability as the combustion-powered versions, the Defender Sport’s EMA setup utilizes underfloor batteries. JLR’s Mark Cameron, who heads up the Discovery and Defender brands, admitted that there may be a slight reduction in wheel travel and articulation versus a full-size Defender.

Then again, few owners are using the full capabilities of their Defenders on the regular, even if they really are landed English gentry roving around their untamed huge tracts of land. A lot of the Defender’s ability isn’t just mechanical doggedness, like an old Series Land Rover, but clever terrain-management software. All of that suite of abilities should port over.

See all results for Land Rover Defender Sport for sale near 53206

A smaller Defender, even one that’s perhaps not quite ready to take on the Dakar Rally, does sound like plenty of fun, especially on narrower trails. Given how successful the current Defender model has been for JLR as a whole, it probably can’t get here fast enough.

#4374. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

#4373. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

Earlier this month, Tesla made the surprise announcement that it would wind down production of the polarizing Cybertruck in the middle of next year. A culprit for the Cybertruck’s demise was a much smaller Tesla, the Cybercab, a tiny two-door pod designed to be autonomous and already running as a robotaxi in a few locations. There are some caveats. That isn’t the final price, as Cybercab owners will also need to pay $299 per month to operate the vehicle, and the Cybercab is currently only able to operate in select geofenced areas, reportedly the same regions where Tesla’s Robotaxi service currently runs. #4371. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#4368. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

#4366. 10 Games That Made Me Weirdly Passionate About Jobs I'd Never Want

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

Some of my favourite games are, when you really think about it, just jobs. I have pressure-washed patios, stamped passports, hauled cargo across half of Europe and sold second-hand books out of a trailer, all of it voluntarily and in my free time. And boy, did I take every single one of them seriously!

The Best Cozy Games That You Need to Play in Fall 2026 feature autumnal settings and the distinctive vibes of the season.

The funny thing is that I wouldn't actually want any of these jobs. Some of them look like far too much hard work, others require a kind of patience I most definitely do not possess, and with one or two, I'm fairly certain I'd end up in prison. That is probably exactly what makes them so enjoyable from the safety of my sofa, so let's take a look at the ten games that made me weirdly passionate about jobs I'd never want.

I had sunk many hours into both PowerWash Simulator games long before I ever held an actual pressure washer. That finally changed earlier this year, and I'm pleased to report that watching grime disappear is just as satisfying in real life as it is on screen. On a warm summer's day, it's even quite fun.

Still, there's a lot to be said for staying warm, dry and cozied up on the sofa whilst doing it. The game has an almost meditative quality that I couldn't quite find with a real hose in my hands, and that's no accident. Lead designer Nick McCarthy has said that the team left out certain real-world inconveniences on purpose, and I'm grateful for every single one of them.

FuturLab released the sequel on 23 October 2025, bringing 38 new jobs to Muckingham, online co-op for up to four players and new tools like an abseiling rig and a cherry picker. There are also two kittens named Bubbles and Squeak, which was frankly all the convincing I needed. As an actual career, though, it looks like an awful lot of work, so I'll stick to the version without the wet socks.

Papers, Please's premise is incredibly dark and difficult: you are manning a booth at the border of the fictional Eastern Bloc country of Arstotzka. It's 1982, and as a border inspector, it is your responsibility to check passports, permits and anything else that gets slid across your desk. Make a mistake and you get a wage deduction. Your family, meanwhile, desperately needs that money. The game is, however, also tense and brilliant, and it also taught me that I would be entirely unsuited for the job.

Quite frankly, I'm just not enough of a bootlicker for it. I'm far too nice, and my first instinct is to wave everybody through, which is not something Papers, Please looks kindly upon. Being generous with your stamp sooner or later gets you killed by your own government, and it's hard to build a career on that.

Note: Lucas Pope worked on the Uncharted series at Naughty Dog before making a game that's almost entirely about paperwork.

By its tenth anniversary in 2023, the game had sold over five million copies, so there are clearly plenty of people out there who are much better at saying no than I am. I have a lot of respect for them. I'd just rather not meet them at passport control.

Running a late-night coffee shop in an alternative version of Seattle sounds like a dream. Even more so when you consider that your visitors will consist of elves, orcs and mermaids that are living alongside humans. Coffee is the great connector here, since the need for a warm drink and someone to talk to is universal across every race. Toge Productions chose Seattle because Starbucks first opened there, and also because the rain sets the mood so well. It's easily one of the coziest games I own.

Parts of this job would actually suit me extremely well: I enjoy good banter, I'm perfectly happy with small talk, and I seem to have the kind of approachable face that makes strangers trauma dump on me far more often than you'd expect. If being a barista was only about listening, I'd be employee of the month.

Unfortunately, you also have to make the coffee, and Coffee Talk is the game that showed me just how hilariously bad I am at latte art. Nothing I produce looks like it was made on purpose. So as much as I love the idea, I could never run a coffee shop of my own.

Note: Creator Mohammad Fahmi sadly passed away in March 2022. He pitched the game as holding a warm cup of coffee by a window whilst it rains outside and lo-fi music plays in the background, which is exactly how it feels.

If you're looking for relaxing experiences with guaranteed quality, I recommend these ten little-known cozy games from famous developers.

Stardew Valley is meant to be about running a cute little farm with cute little animals on it. The way I play it, with spreadsheets at the ready and more wiki tabs open than I'd like to admit, has very little to do with that. My approach is a lot closer to a general planning a war than a farmer enjoying the countryside.

The forensic intensity I bring to this game does scare me a little. Every day is planned, every crop has to earn its place, and my poor character hasn't had a quiet afternoon in years. If I ran a real farm like that, I'd work myself into a burnout before the first harvest.

Note: Eric Barone, better known as ConcernedApe, made Stardew Valley on his own over roughly four years.

The game turned ten on 26 February 2026 and has sold around 50 million copies. I'd love to know how many of those players are peacefully watering their parsnips and enjoying the sunset, and how many are like me. I have my suspicions.

Something happens to me whenever I open Euro Truck Simulator 2. Within minutes, I turn into a 60-year-old trucker who has been doing this for decades, completely locked in, with nothing on my mind except my cargo and the motorway ahead. I can't explain it, but it awakens something in me.

There are two wolves inside of me: One is a sweet softie, and the other one is a fourth-generation trucker that graduated from the school of hard knocks, living and breathing 18-wheelers. Sadly for the second wolf, I'm really, really bad at parking, and truth be told, I'm no better at it in the game. That feels like a bit of a dealbreaker for a job that ends with reversing a trailer into a loading bay.

SCS Software first released the game at retail in autumn 2012, before it arrived on Steam on 16 January 2013. By its tenth birthday, it had sold over 13 million copies, and players had bought DLC more than 80 million times. Clearly, I'm not the only one with a trucker wolf, so at least I'm in good company.

Exterminauts is an upcoming co-op shooter from Behaviour Interactive, the studio behind Dead by Daylight, and it hands you several jobs at once. As part of a crew of three, you clock in, take on MegaCorp contracts, repair what's broken and exterminate alien pests along the way. It was revealed at gamescom Opening Night Live in August 2026 and is planned for 2027.

Anyone who has watched me deal with a woodlouse or a spider knows that pest control isn't my calling. I'm quite a caring person, so I had a lot of fun with the healing side of things. I've also discovered that I'm alarmingly quick to shoot my own teammates, sometimes because they were being annoying, and sometimes entirely by accident.

Note: Friendly fire is on in Exterminauts, and swinging one of the bigger weapons around carelessly is enough to take a teammate down.

A colleague who keeps taking out the rest of the crew isn't much use to anyone, no matter how good her healing is. I can't imagine it going down well in a performance review, either. It's better for everyone if I stay off the payroll.

Subnautica is one of my favourite games of all time, which means I approach the deep ocean with a healthy dose of suspicion. Dave the Diver has done nothing but confirm that this is the correct attitude. You spend your days diving into the Blue Hole to catch fish, and the further down you go, the more things would like to eat you instead.

Once the sun sets, the second job begins, and you help chef Bancho run the sushi restaurant, serving customers and keeping the drinks coming. All of that after a full day of nearly being eaten by sharks! I’d be a horrible sushi tester on the basis of not liking fish, and I could also never be the waiter on the basis of lacking a good sense of balance.

Note: The restaurant is the idea of Dave's friend Cobra, a former arms dealer who now handles the business side of things. Naturally.

By September 2026, Dave the Diver had sold more than 10 million copies across all platforms, and I completely understand why. It's a wonderful game. It's also the best argument I've ever seen for staying on dry land and ordering takeaway.

A review of over the hill, a cozy exploration-focused driving game.

Kerbal Space Program puts you in charge of a space program run by the Kerbals, little green aliens who are far braver than they have any right to be. You build rockets, launch them and watch most of them explode. I was oddly passionate about all of it, right up until the moment I finally made it into orbit.

I'm very aware that the game doesn't end there. It had taken me so long to reach that one milestone, though, that my passion fizzled out on the spot, and I decided that my work here was done. That's quite unusual for me, as I'm normally someone who needs to tick off every last goal.

A real head of a space program with that attitude wouldn't bode well for anyone. NASA worked with developer Squad on an asteroid mission update in 2014, and ESA followed with missions of its own in 2020, so the people who do this for a living are clearly made of sterner stuff than I am. I have a lot of respect for them, and I'm more than happy to watch from the ground.

Barbie Rewind was developed by Digital Eclipse, published by Atari and released on 12 November 2026. It is unfathomably fun. You get to decorate the DreamHouse with over 250 pieces of furniture and decor inspired by real Barbie playsets, from a classic pink vanity to a '90s inflatable chair. There are also 16 classic Barbie games from 1991 to 2007 included, one of which, Barbie: Vacation Adventure, had never been released before.

Truth be told, I think I'd make a good interior designer, and I think I'd enjoy it, too. In Barbie Rewind, you get to design to your heart's content, and nobody questions your choices. Ken, Teresa and Christie do pop in to ask for help, but none of them will ever tell you that your sofa is ugly.

Real clients are a different story. Even when something looks questionable at best, you have to go with the flow and keep them happy, and whilst you'd hope they trust your design decisions, there's absolutely no guarantee that they will. I don't think I have the temperament for that, and I'm fairly sure someone would end up wounded.

In Tiny Bookshop, you leave everything behind to sell second-hand books out of a little trailer in the seaside town of Bookstonbury-by-the-Sea. Each morning, you pick a spot, stock your shelves and wait for the locals to wander in. Many of the books are real ones, which I love.

I've worked in retail before, I'm quite a good salesperson, and I enjoy helping people find what they're looking for. The customers in Tiny Bookshop put that to the test, because a fair few of them behave as if it's their very first day on Earth. Not all of them, mind you, but enough of them describe the book they want so vaguely that it borders on nonsensical.

On top of that, everyone in town seems to need a favour. Community is important, of course, but I'm trying to run a bookshop here, and I'd quite like to be left alone to do it! Over half a million players have fallen in love with Tiny Bookshop, and it won three German Developer Awards in 2025, so this one might just be a me problem. I'd still end up scaring all of my customers away.

Frontier Developments returns to the animal park with Planet Zoo 2.

#4365. AI supercharges laser physics with a stunning 250x speed boost

Simulating the complex behavior of light inside powerful laser systems requires enormous computing resources, making it difficult for researchers to predict and adjust laser performance quickly. Now, scientists at Stanford University, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have developed an artificial intelligence model that dramatically accelerates these calculations. Using deep learning, the new approach reproduces the results of conventional simulations in a fraction of the time while maintaining high accuracy across a wide variety of laser pulse shapes.

The advance focuses on a branch of physics called second-order nonlinear optics, also known as χ2 processes. These interactions occur when light waves exchange energy while traveling through specially designed crystals, allowing scientists to change the frequency of light and precisely control the shape of laser pulses. Such capabilities are particularly important at large scientific facilities that use lasers to generate intense X-rays.

How Laser Light Helps Generate Powerful X-Rays

At SLAC's upgraded Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS-II), laser pulses undergo a series of transformations before they can help produce X-rays. Infrared light is first converted into green light and then into ultraviolet (UV) light. The resulting UV pulse strikes a cathode, releasing a cluster of electrons that is accelerated and manipulated to generate powerful X-ray pulses.

The precise timing and shape of the UV pulse help determine the characteristics of the electron bunch. Those characteristics, in turn, influence the quality of the X-rays that researchers use in scientific experiments. Accurately predicting the conversion of light between different frequencies is therefore an important part of optimizing the system.

The new AI approach, described in the journal Advanced Photonics, was developed specifically to model the nonlinear χ2 interactions involved in this frequency conversion process.

AI Replaces Time-Consuming Laser Calculations

Traditionally, scientists simulate these interactions by solving a complex mathematical equation known as the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A widely used technique called the split-step Fourier method (SSFM) calculates how light changes as it travels through a material, repeatedly switching between representations of the pulse in time and frequency.

Although the method produces accurate results, it demands substantial computing power. In the complete laser simulation examined by the researchers, this calculation alone accounts for approximately 95 percent of the total processing time.

To overcome that bottleneck, the team developed an AI model based on a type of recurrent neural network called LSTM (long short-term memory). Building on earlier research that used similar networks to predict how laser pulses travel through optical fibers, the scientists adapted the approach to handle more complicated interactions involving multiple light waves.

They tested the model using a process called noncollinear sum frequency generation, or SFG, in which three interconnected light fields evolve together inside a crystal. The simulations covered a wide variety of laser pulse shapes, providing a demanding test of the model's ability to reproduce complex optical behavior.

One important innovation was the way the AI handles information. Rather than repeatedly converting calculations between time and frequency, as conventional simulations do, the neural network works entirely with a compressed representation of the light's frequency characteristics. This eliminates much of the repetitive computation that makes traditional methods slow.

Complex Laser Simulations in Just Milliseconds

The results showed that the AI model could accurately recreate how laser pulses change over time and across different frequencies, even under particularly challenging conditions. These included pulses with pronounced gaps in their frequency spectra and strong variations in optical phase.

When the researchers processed multiple simulations together using graphics processing units, the average calculation time for each simulation dropped to just a few milliseconds. That represents an improvement of orders of magnitude over conventional methods, making it possible to obtain predictions far more quickly without substantially compromising accuracy.

The system also demonstrated an important ability to capture the interconnected behavior of the light waves. When the AI accurately predicted the main output of the SFG process, its predictions for the other interacting fields were generally accurate as well. This suggests that the network learned important features of the overall interaction rather than simply reproducing one output.

Toward Smarter Lasers and Real-Time Control

Beyond faster simulations, the researchers envision connecting AI models directly to operating laser systems. Their approach uses a modular design in which individual physical processes can be represented by separate trained neural networks. Combining these models could make it possible to predict the behavior of an entire experimental system while it is running.

One potential application is the creation of digital twins, detailed virtual models that mirror the behavior of real laser equipment. With sufficiently fast and accurate predictions, these systems could help researchers monitor experiments, anticipate changes, and adjust laser settings in response to changing conditions.

The technology could also support adaptive laser control and closer integration with diagnostic instruments that measure the results of experiments. By removing a major computational obstacle, the research brings the possibility of more responsive, precisely controlled laser systems closer to reality, with potential benefits for a wide range of scientific facilities that rely on powerful lasers.

Materials provided by SPIE--International Society for Optics and Photonics. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4364. The Best Made-in-USA Gifts for Every Person on Your Shopping List

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

From trusted tools to road-trip essentials, we rounded up the toughest gear made in the United States for the car people in your life.

This article was updated in November 2026 with new products and information.

There’s a particular satisfaction in picking up a tool or piece of gear and knowing where it was made. It’s more than patriotism: a pair of boots stitched in Michigan or a kitchen tool forged in Ohio carries a connection to the people and skills behind it.

Buying American-made products helps support the craftspeople, businesses, and communities that keep making things here. And finding those products doesn’t have to be a treasure hunt. We’ve rounded up standout U.S.-made picks for weekend wrenchers, road-trip warriors, and everyone in between.

The brass bolsters and wood handle give the iconic Buck Knives 110 Folding Hunter Knife a significant heft that exudes quality. Made in Post Falls, Idaho, it locks open with a satisfying click and holds an edge through serious cutting tasks. It is not the most high-tech blade on the market, but it is a timeless tool that feels great in the hand.

Most carry-on bags feel flimsy, but the Pelican ATX 22 feels like you could drag it behind the car on the highway and it would survive. Hell, I'm not even sure a particularly grumpy baggage handler could destroy this thing.

The layout is simple, but the injection-molded construction is undeniably Pelican. This particular model is sized just right to fit in the overhead bin without a fight, and you can rest assured clothes and gear will be protected from the elements better than standard fabric luggage ever could manage.

Built just down the road from me in Rockford, Michigan, these Wolverine 1000 Mile Boots are no joke. While they do require a significant break-in period, the payoff is worth the blister or two.

Once the Horween leather molds to your foot, these boots feel like a second skin that look as good as they feel and are tough enough for daily wear. The Goodyear welt construction also means you can resole them in a few years rather than tossing them in the trash when the tread wears down.

As you'd expect from a brand as synonymous with quality as Channellock, this Tool Roll-5 is the kind of pliers kit that just works, day in and day out. The cutters bite cleanly, the tongue-and-groove jaws actually meet, and the pivots don't wobble after a season of real use.

The included roll keeps everything from clanking around in the trunk or bottoming out in a drawer and is great for keeping forgetful DIYers such as myself from losing them in the middle of projects. As all products on this list, these tools are made in the USA and tough enough to hand to a neighbor without worrying about getting them back bent.

Manufactured in the US, the Smithey 5.5-quart dutch oven skips the fragile enamel coatings found on expensive European imports in favor of bare, heavily seasoned cast iron. You can drag it across steel grill grates or bury it directly in glowing campfire coals without worrying about chipping a delicate finish. And it works equally well atop gas, electric, and induction stovetops.

The sheer mass of the walls and dome lid acts like a thermal battery, locking in steady, even heat for hours to properly break down tough cuts of meat and soften even the most stubborn carrots. It’s a heavy-duty, straightforward piece of American hardware that handles campfire stews and kitchen braises with equal capability.

If you're looking to pair the Dutch oven with a skillet, or simply don't need the massive capacity of a 5.5-quart pot, the Smithey No. 10 is the logical alternative. Like the rest of their South Carolina-forged lineup, it features a machined, glass-smooth interior that eliminates the stubborn break-in period typical of modern cast iron. It cooks with the non-stick capability of a well-worn vintage piece right out of the box.

The 10-inch diameter hits the sweet spot for daily duty, whether you're searing a pair of ribeyes over an open fire or frying eggs on a kitchen stove, although there are plenty of other sizes available on Smithey's website if you're hoping to go smaller or larger. I'd also recommend picking up a chainmail scrubber to get out the more stubborn food remnants, and Smithey's salt keeper is an adorable accessory to boot.

Having a heavy-duty piece of American metal that takes high heat without warping, wipes clean in seconds, and feels substantial enough to outlast your vehicle fundamentally changes how you operate in the kitchen.

The GoRuck GR1 is overkill for a commute, which is exactly why you will like it. Made in America by a veteran-owned company, this bag has straps that are padded perfectly to handle heavy loads, and the laptop compartment is suspended to protect your tech from drops. It opens flat for easy packing and shrugs off rain and abrasions like they are nothing.

I've personally owned one of these for more than 15 years now, and it's been everything from a daily backpack in college to a tool bag that's been used and abused during car repairs. While the 1000D Cordura is certainly faded and the zipper pulls have been replaced a few times, it still performs just as it did on day one.

Finding quality local products oftentimes requires giving up a Saturday morning. You have to navigate a farmer's market, walk the stalls, and sift through the inventory to find something worthwhile. The Farmers Finds outsources that legwork by scouring regional markets across the country, buying small-batch goods from independent makers, and packing them into a single box. It’s a straightforward logistical solution akin to a regional community supported agriculture (CSA) box. Instead of driving across state lines to find a specific local preserve or hot sauce, it arrives directly on your porch.You can order a single box, though the subscription model is how the service is really meant to be used. The monthly tier delivers two to four items from a single brand, while the quarterly option scales up to seven to ten products sourced from five different makers. It's a practical gift for someone who appreciates regional goods, but doesn't have the bandwidth to track down the vendors themselves. You get quality American-made products, and the makers get the business.

What more can I say about Duck Tape Duct Tape that hasn't already been said? Sure, it's never a long-term solution to automotive or home problems, but it'll get the job done until you find a more permanent solution. Hopefully you'll never have to use it, but for 10 bucks or so, it's nice insurance to throw in the trunk for the inevitable emergency.

The Wave is one of Leatherman's most iconic tools, and while it takes on a new shape with the Wave Alpha, it's still the answer when you want one thing that handles 10 small jobs and you don't feel like going back to the toolbox.

This all-in-one tool features one-hand blades, real pliers, actual drivers, a large scissor tool, and more. Leatherman backs it with a no-drama warranty, and their stuff is easy to service if you get it gritty (I've sent in my original Wave for service twice and had it back within a week with little more than the shipping cost to send it out).

Odds are this tool will outlast whoever you give it to, so consider it a long-term investment made right here in the United States.

If you want deep color and gloss for a weekend cruiser, this Griot's Garage Best of Show Wax gets the job done. Formulated just west of Indianapolis, Indiana, it goes on smooth and buffs off without leaving stubborn white dust in the panel gaps.

While it's easy enough to use with a hand buff, it works equally well with an electric buffer if you want to expedite the process. It's affordable, it works well, and overall it delivers a robust shine with a little bit of elbow grease.

Duke Cannon's Big Ass Brick of Soap is comically big at first, but then you realize it outlasts three normal ones and doesn't turn into goo in the shower. I've purchased and used a dozen of these over the last decade, and every time I go through a single bar, my spouse has already gone through a three-pack of normal ones.

The scent of this particular bar (they have dozens of scents/formulations to choose from) is more warm "vanilla/wood" than "spill at the distillery," but it does have that signature bourbon smell you'd expect from a little Buffalo Trace.

This Rite in the Rain notepad lets you write down torque values, weird part numbers, or your "What's that noise?" notes, all without having to worry about whether the pages will smear if your hands are greasy or it's misting outside.

The covers hold up in a pocket, and the wire doesn't explode into a tangle like some other cheap pads I've used over the years. It's a bit pricey for a small notepad, but when you need a reliable notepad that can take on the elements and solvents, you won't find a better option.

As a Michigander, I'm a bit biased, but Carhartt Beanies are just a way of life (second only to Stormy Kromers). While not all versions are made in America, there are Woodside Beanies made right here in the States. Just be sure to check the product listing to confirm before making your purchase.

This American-made bag takes a beating and looks all the better for it. The rugged twill of the Filson Original Briefcase resists water and wear, while the bridle leather handles soften up nicely over time. It is heavy for what it holds, but it protects a laptop and documents with a style that works as well in a truck as it does in an office.

LED technology revived the classic Maglite form factor you remember from your childhood. Built in Ontario, California, it still has the heft that feels reassuring in your hand, but now it throws a beam that properly lights up the road ahead (or engine beneath you). You get a simple focus twist mechanism, as well as the convenience of D-cell batteries that are easy enough to find at any gas station.

Smell like you upgraded to a nicer car. Drift infuses a magnetized wood block with clean-ingredient essential oils—teak, amber, and cedar—then snaps it to a low-profile metal visor clip. It's made in the U.S., looks grown-up, and takes quick monthly refill blocks when the scent fades. No dangling trees, no headaches.

Pouring fluids into a cramped engine bay usually results in a mess, but this FlexAll Flexible Funnel by TEC Products solves that geometry problem.

The nitrile rubber handles oil and gas without degrading, and you can mold it around hoses and wires to create a leak-free path. Sure, it might be a bit more of a hassle to clean when you're done, but the convenience of the gooseneck makes all the difference when trying to get fluids into all the nooks and crannies of modern vehicles.

The lifetime warranty is real, but the comfort is why you will keep buying them. Knit in Northfield, Vermont, these Darn Tough Micro Crew Socks breathe well inside a driving shoe or a heavy boot, and the merino wool blend doesn't stink after a long day on the road.

You will have a hard time wearing a hole in a pair, which makes the higher price tag feel like a bargain over the long haul. I've had probably a dozen pair of Darn Tough socks over the years, and I only managed to wear a hole in one, which was only thanks to a little nail sticking out of my home's mid-century wood floors. And, of course, Darn Tough promptly replaced it with a brand-new pair.

You usually buy emergency kits hoping you wasted your money, because nobody wants to have to use one. But when you get stranded on a dark shoulder, this Pelican SRVL2 2-Person Emergency Kit is exactly what you want to have in the cargo area.

Made and assembled in Torrance, California, this kit organizes the chaos of emergency prep (water pouches, food rations, and first-aid gear) into a distinct, bombproof case that protects the contents from moisture or being crushed. You can toss it in the trunk and forget about it until the moment you really need it.

The integrated handles and wheels are great for easy transfer between cars or garages and the neatly organized bags, and instructions inside all but ensure you'll be better prepared than anyone in the neighborhood if you ever do end up needing it.

According to the FTC, a product must be “all or virtually all” made in the United States. That means final assembly and significant processing happen in the USA, and nearly all components are made and sourced in the USA.

No. “Assembled in the USA” means the product was put together in the USA, but some parts may come from other countries.

Look for the product’s country-of-origin information and check the manufacturer’s website for details about where it is made, assembled, and sourced.

There are a lot of reasons why, but mainly because shopping U.S.-made goods means you are supporting domestic manufacturers, workers, supply chains.

Gannon Burgett loves cameras, cars, and coffee: a perfect combination for his Hearst Autos work. His byline has appeared in USA Today, Gizmodo, TechCrunch, Digital Trends, the Detroit Free Press, and more.
